articles.abstract: Characterizing biodiversity around offshore infrastructure is necessary to assess possible influences of industrial activities on marine communities and distinguish persistent ecological change from short-term variability. Combining environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding with autonomous sampling offers a way to expand biological, spatial and temporal coverage while reducing dependence on crewed field operations. We evaluated this approach around a floating production, storage and offloading unit (FPSO) in the Santos Basin, Brazil, to establish an initial biodiversity reference and inform subsequent monitoring. A third-generation Environmental Sample Processor integrated into the W Tupan II uncrewed surface vessel enabled autonomous water sampling at coastal sites, transit locations and the FPSO area, yielding 64 biological samples. We used mitochondrial 12S and 16S metabarcoding to assess taxonomic diversity, sampling completeness and spatial and short-term temporal variation. Around the FPSO, 47 samples from 21 points detected 34 species with 12S and 28 with 16S, representing 74.3% and 65.4% of the respective estimated species richness. Local analyses showed weak radial differentiation across 300-1,500 m around the FPSO, with no near-far taxonomic indicators remaining significant after multiple-testing corrections. Samples collected at the same point approximately 1-2 h apart were almost as dissimilar as samples from different points, whereas technical replicates of post-extraction processing closely matched their source DNA profiles. Taxon turnover accounted for approximately 73% and 80% of temporal Jaccard dissimilarity for 12S and 16S, respectively. Regional analyses recovered a coastal-offshore compositional contrast, with geography and sampling date jointly represented. This pilot supports autonomous eDNA sampling as an operational approach to offshore biodiversity monitoring. The findings favour repeated sampling across campaigns to distinguish transient detections from recurrent patterns and persistent compositional changes.

articles.title: BenchMHC: a reproducible framework for peptide-MHC presentation prediction
articles.abstract: Predicting which peptides an MHC molecule presents is the first step in neoantigen and epitope discovery pipelines. Most published predictors are released for inference only, and each is trained on a different dataset, so the effect of a new method cannot be separated from the effect of its training data. We present BenchMHC, an open framework that reproduces, retrains and evaluates pMHC presentation models on public data only, and that records every implementation decision made in a reproduction. Our NetMHCpan-4.1 reproduction reaches 0.794 per-allele Mean Top-K against 0.790 for the official webserver, and 0.0025 Median FRANK against 0.0022. It scores 280,000 peptide/allele pairs in 27 s, about 350 times faster than the original binary. We then examine the training data. In the public NetMHCpan-4.1 eluted-ligand sets, 86 to 99% of hits are found in the human proteome, against about 12% of their decoys, so a model can separate hits from decoys using this difference rather than features related to MHC binding. Redrawing the decoys within the source protein of each hit and matching their cysteine status, with no other change, raises per-allele Mean Top-K on the regenerated v2.0.0 evaluation set from 0.734 to 0.755, and increases Median FRANK on CD8 epitopes from 0.0025 to 0.0053. The same change improves one evaluation set and degrades the other. Code (Apache-2.0) and model checkpoints (CC BY-NC-4.0): https://github.com/instadeepai/BenchMHC-public.

articles.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Transcriptomic Data Analysis and Visualization: Multi-Model Workflow Evaluation
articles.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive benchmarking evaluation of large language models(LLMs) and agentic coding systems for automated analysis and visualization workflows for transcriptomic data, in particular human responses to COVID-19 infection. Multiple models, including ChatGPT 5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1, and Llama4-Scout, were assessed across a series of scientific prompts designed to test their ability to reproduce workflow components such as dimensionality reduction, clustering, outlier detection, reproducibility, and code generation. The benchmark protocol involved varying prompt specificity and examined both quantitative metrics such as clustering scores and outlier counts as well as qualitative aspects such as code quality and reproducibility. Results indicate that prompt specificity improves code structure and methodological correctness, but quantitative performance depends heavily on preprocessing choices and execution environment. While some models produced strong code and reproducible outputs, alignment with scientific targets like label-based clustering was inconsistent. The findings highlight the promise and limitations of current LLMs for automating scientific data analysis and visualization and suggest directions for future benchmarking and workflow standardization.

articles.title: Best Practices for Pre-Processing Large-Scale ATAC-Seq Data: Why Epidemiological Studies Demand Greater Stringency
articles.abstract: Assay for transposase accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) and related techniques provide critical insight into the epigenetic mechanisms that regulate gene expression in health and disease. Accurate identification of biologically meaningful chromatin accessibility signals remains an underexplored analytical challenge. Advances in sequencing technologies have increased both the magnitude and complexity of ATAC-seq datasets, leading to demand for scalable, reproducible and robust computational analysis frameworks. Peak calling, which identifies regions of chromatin accessibility, is a critical step that underpins all downstream quantitative analyses. However, there is a lack of consensus regarding the optimal peak calling strategy. Here, we present a novel bioinformatics pipeline PIPPA (Pipeline for Integrative Peak calling in Population-scale ATAC-seq), for quality control and peak set curation of large-scale ATAC-seq datasets. Using two independent cell-type sorted ATAC-seq datasets, we show that peak calling performance is dataset-dependent and that no single significance threshold performs optimally across all scenarios. We provide practical recommendations for parameters to generate high-confidence chromatin accessibility profiles. Our peak calling approach is applicable for other genome wide epigenomic assays such as ChIP-seq and CUT&Tag. By standardising this process, the PIPPA pipeline enhances epidemiological studies focused in identifying epigenetic dysregulation associated with development and disease.

articles.title: Bird-assisted sampling of air temperature reveals three-dimensional cooling effects of urban vegetation
articles.abstract: Air temperature in cities is highly variable horizontally and vertically, reflecting the complexity of the urban landscape. Yet, studies of urban temperature still depend largely on ground-based meteorological stations and satellite-derived surface temperature products, both of which provide limited information on near-surface air conditions and vertical structure. We tested a bio-assisted monitoring approach to characterise fine-scale three-dimensional patterns of summer air temperature in the city of Rome, Italy, using homing pigeons (Columba livia) equipped with lightweight GPS loggers air-temperature sensors. Flight data collected during summer sampling campaigns between 2023 and 2025 revealed pronounced spatial, vertical, and temporal variability in air temperature over the urban area. Modelling results showed that vegetation had a measurable cooling influence within the lower urban atmosphere with grass cover and wooded patches were both associated with lower air temperatures. Thermal contrasts between land-cover types were the strongest at low altitudes and during morning hours, when air above artificial surfaces was up to approximately 5 {degrees}C warmer than above vegetated areas. We also observed a buffering effect associated with green areas: air temperature, particularly near wooded vegetation, remained relatively stable up to approximately 300 m from the patch edge before increasing by as much as 3 {degrees}C. These findings suggest that animal-borne sensing can complement conventional monitoring by capturing air temperature variability across urban landscapes and heights, while also helping to identify when and where urban vegetation most effectively mitigates heat exposure. This approach offers new opportunities to support climate-resilient urban planning and targeted heat mitigation strategies.

articles.title: Brain Age Gap Associations with Externalising Behaviours in Youth: A Longitudinal Investigation in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Cohort
articles.abstract: Background. Early adolescence is a period of heightened risk for the emergence of externalising psychopathology, making it an important window for identifying neurodevelopmental risk markers. Differences between predicted brain age and chronological age - termed the brain age gap - reflect variation from age-typical patterns of brain structure. While brain age gap has been closely linked with internalising behaviours in adolescence, less is known about its relationship with externalising symptoms. This study examined whether brain age gap in late childhood/early adolescence (9-11 years) is associated with current externalising symptoms and whether it predicts externalising trajectories over seven-year follow-up. Methods. Participants were 10,516 adolescents (aged 9-11 at baseline; up to 18 years at follow-up) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study who met inclusion/exclusion criteria. Brain age gap for each participant was derived from an external validated prediction model (Drobinin et al., 2022) applied to baseline measurements of cortical volume, area, and subcortical volume. Linear mixed-effects models were used to test cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between baseline brain age gap and externalising symptoms, as assessed using the Child Behaviour Checklist. Primary models were adjusted for age, sex, pubertal status, and prior to inclusion of sociodemographic covariates (ethnoracial identity and caregiver highest education). Results. A higher/more positive brain age gap was associated with greater externalising symptoms at baseline (B[SE]=0.067[0.033], p=.042), but this association was removed following sociodemographic adjustment (B[SE]=0.056[0.033], p=.088). Longitudinally, a significant brain age gap x age interaction was identified that remained evident after sociodemographic adjustment, with this relationship weakening across adolescence (B[SE]=-0.007[0.003], p=.033). Conclusions. These findings suggest that a more positive brain age gap, indicating more mature-appearing brain structure for age, in late childhood/early adolescence may be associated with externalising psychopathology, but this relationship is likely to be age- and context-dependent rather than a stable marker of persistent behavioural risk. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. National Institutes of Health, R01AA030575, K24AA031052

articles.title: CATFISHR: integration of transcriptome and inferred CNV profiles for comprehensive malignant cell identification
articles.abstract: Malignant cell identification in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) remains challenging because transcriptomic cell typing, somatic variant detection and inferred copy-number approaches each have modality-specific limitations. Rare or ambiguous malignant populations are especially vulnerable to misclassification or exclusion, despite their relevance to treatment resistance, minimal residual disease, and metastasis. We developed CATFISHR, a semi-automated workflow that integrates RNA-expression similarity, inferred copy-number variation (CNV) profiles, and consensus cell typing to classify malignant cells relative to high-confidence references. CATFISHR was evaluated across eight cohorts, including seven scRNA-seq datasets spanning multiple carcinomas and melanoma subtypes, and one 10x Visium spatial transcriptomics sample. Compared with available benchmarks or ground truths, CATFISHR achieved balanced accuracy > 0.85 in six of eight cohorts and F1 score > 0.80 in six of eight cohorts. Cells uniquely identified by CATFISHR as malignant ("Hidden" cells) were present in every dataset and were not consistently explained by standard quality-control metrics. In several cohorts, Hidden cells were transcriptionally closer to benchmark malignant than non-malignant compartments; in Visium data, sampled Hidden spots contained histologist-confirmed morphologically malignant cells. CATFISHR reduces missed malignant calls while preserving rare, transitional and benchmark-discordant populations for downstream investigation.

articles.title: Cancer cells acquire cysteine directly from a reduced tumor microenvironment
articles.abstract: The metabolic environment of a tumor is shaped by the nutrients available in its interstitial fluid, yet the redox composition of that fluid is poorly defined. Measuring sulfur metabolites in the interstitial fluid of tumors, matched healthy organs, and serum across three mouse models of cancer, we find that the tumor microenvironment (TME) is a chemically reduced compartment in which free cysteine predominates over its oxidized form, cystine. This is especially pronounced in the lung TME, where cystine is nearly absent. We further show that lung cancer cells take up cysteine and cystine with comparable efficiency and proliferate on cysteine alone, and that the abundant glutathione in the TME helps keep cysteine reduced through disulfide exchange. In a medium formulated to match the sulfur composition of the lung tumor interstitial fluid, cells become independent of cystine import through xCT. Cells cultured in this medium were resistant to glutaminase inhibitors, oxidants and ferroptosis inducers, and better maintained NADPH levels under oxidative challenge. These findings suggest that standard culture conditions overestimate the dependence of cancer cells on cystine uptake and their vulnerability to oxidative stress-targeting therapies.

articles.title: Cerebello-basal ganglia networks and behavior across adulthood and aging
articles.abstract: The cerebellum contributes to aging, cognition, and reward related processing, but has been relatively understudied in these domains. The cerebello-basal ganglia (CB-BG) circuit may be key to better understanding how the brain ages. Prior work has implicated this circuit in aging in a small sample, though it is also of interest in age-related neurodegenerative disease, particularly Parkinson's Disease. Here, we investigated the CB-BG network, which has been implicated in modulation of cognitive, motor, and reward-related functions. In a sample of 138 participants between the ages of 35 and 86 we looked at network connectivity in cognitive and motor sub-circuits. Participants completed motor and cognitive testing batteries followed by 26 minutes of resting state functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging (fcMRI). This data was analyzed using the CONN toolbox with an ROI-ROI approach targeting the CB-BG circuit. We replicated the previously mapped cognitive subcircuit and motor subcircuits. When examining connectivity by age group (early and late middle age and older adult hood), we found higher functional connectivity in early middle age compared to older adulthood, with no results related to late middle age. Analysis of connectivity as it relates to performance on the Stroop task showed higher connectivity-behavior associations in early middle-aged adults compared to older adults. We also explored sex differences and found higher functional connectivity in females compared to males. Analysis of steroid hormone levels revealed higher connectivity associated with progesterone in females relative to males. Together, we have replicated motor and cognitive CB-BG subcircuits and further demonstrated that this network has altered connectivity associated with age, sex, progesterone, and cognitive performance. This expanded investigation of CB-BG networks represents an essential new step in increasing our knowledge of age-related cognitive and motor declines and may be particularly relevant for consideration in Parkinson's Disease. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. National Institute on Aging, https://ror.org/049v75w11, R01AG064010, R01AG064010

articles.title: Cerebral Organization in the trilobite Yunnanocephalus yunnanensis
articles.abstract: The clade Trilobita is recognized for its extraordinary morphological diversifications amidst a highly constrained body plan. This raises the question of whether trilobite nervous systems were conservative or comparably diverse. However, despite the identification of thousands of trilobite species and increasing evidence for neural preservation in other Paleozoic euarthropods, the recognition of a fossilized trilobite brain has remained elusive. Here we describe the identification of a trilobite brain and its spatially constrained position within its cranidium. An unusually preserved specimen of the lower Cambrian trilobite Yunnanocephalus yunnanensis reveals a bilaterally organized organ connected to its lateral eyes. Comparisons to the brain of a trilobitomorph xandarellid support the interpretation of this organ as a modest cerebrum comprising prosocerebral, protocerebral, and deutocerebral domains, an organization typifying the euarthropod cerebral ground pattern. These findings suggest that the cerebrum of Yunnanocephalus could have supported the multimodal sensory processing and behavioral repertoires of trilobites, while retaining the deep evolutionary conservation of brain organization across euarthropod lineages

articles.title: Chromosome-level Atlantic switchgrass assemblies reveal a supernumerary B-Chromosome with transcriptional and evolutionary impacts
articles.abstract: Supernumerary B-Chromosomes are extra genetic elements that frequently deviate from Mendelian inheritance to ensure their own survival. Their evolutionary origins and biological impacts within natural plant populations remain largely unexplored. Switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) is a model for studies of local adaptation, but reliance on a single reference genome has limited the detection of lineage-specific genomic content. We generated chromosome-level genome assemblies from the diverged Atlantic switchgrass subpopulation and discovered a previously undetected genomic element: a ~34 Mb supernumerary B-Chromosome, validated by Hi-C contact mapping and long-read depth, which indicates two to four B copies per nucleus. The B-Chromosome has a bipartite architecture including a gene-rich, single-copy proximal region (~8 Mb) and a repeat-rich, gene-poor distal region (~27 Mb) dominated by LTR/Ty3 (Gypsy) elements and punctuated by Mutator TIR peaks. High-resolution mapping reveals a highly rearranged chimera of fragments from multiple autosomes, biased toward the N-subgenome. Intact LTR retrotransposons on the B-Chromosome are younger than those on the A-Chromosomes, especially in its distal region, consistent with a B-Chromosome that arose and expanded within the Atlantic lineage. Population screening and phylogenetic analysis indicate that the B-Chromosome is largely restricted to the Atlantic subpopulation and likely has a single origin. In a typical family, 70% of open-pollinated progeny of B-positive maternal plants were B-positive, with substantial variation among families. Finally, B-Chromosome presence is associated with expression differences in A-Chromosome genes that differ between genetic backgrounds. Together, our results show how accessory chromosomes contribute to the evolutionary and genomic diversity of natural plant populations.

articles.title: Daylight exposure improves sleep and subsequent sleepiness
articles.abstract: Study Objectives: The causal effects of daylight exposure on sleep remain poorly understood, particularly under real-world conditions. This study aimed to address this gap by examining the effects of an afternoon daylight intervention on subsequent sleep. Methods: Ten healthy participants (4 males; 19 to 28 years) completed two randomized 3-h afternoon outdoor walks under high-intensity light (HIL; clear goggles) or attenuated light (AL; neutral-density-filtered goggles; ~10 photopic lux) conditions. Light exposure was centered around the estimated crossover between the phase-advancing and phase-delaying portions of the light phase-response curve, individually determined from baseline dim light melatonin onset (DLMO). Subsequent nocturnal sleep was assessed using at-home polysomnography (PSG), and subjective sleepiness and sleep quality were assessed using the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale and Groningen Sleep Quality Scale, respectively. Differences between conditions and across time were examined using linear mixed-effects models. Results: There were no significant differences between conditions in DLMO timing or the phase angle between DLMO and sleep onset, indicating that the light manipulation did not produce a detectable shift in circadian phase. Sleep duration and self-reported sleep quality were also unchanged. However, nighttime delta power accumulated more rapidly following HIL exposure, accompanied by greater NREM sleep and reduced wakefulness after sleep onset (all p < 0.01). Participants were also significantly less sleepy upon awakening following HIL compared with AL exposure (p < 0.05). Conclusions: High-intensity natural daylight exposure may promote greater sleep intensity and reduce sleepiness upon awakening. These findings highlight a potential role for daytime light exposure in modulating subsequent sleep physiology and next-morning sleepiness, independent of changes in circadian phase.

articles.title: Dimensionality Reduction for Cyclic Compositional Data
articles.abstract: The cyclic nature of many biological systems is frequently reflected in periodic gene expression patterns. Standard dimensionality reductions can reveal such variation but do not link a sample's position on a cycle to an ordering of the molecular features that define it. We introduce clrcycle, which applies a centered log-ratio transformation, learns a cyclic feature ordering by maximizing variance captured by the first Fourier mode, and projects samples onto the corresponding cosine and sine coordinates. The resulting two-dimensional geometry assigns each sample a phase and a radius measuring the magnitude of its projection onto the learned Fourier circle. Across a mouse circadian atlas, clrcycle recovers known temporal organization and reveals tissue-specific differences in rhythmic timing. In FUCCI-profiled single cells, clrcycle represents independently measured cell-cycle phase in two-dimensional coordinates more reliably than conventional two-dimensional embeddings. In human endometrium, a circular coordinate learned from 250 highly variable genes recovers menstrual-stage organization and can stage unseen endometrial biopsies. Together, these results establish clrcycle as powerful, explicitly circular dimensionality reduction technique to quantify high-dimensional cyclic variation across biological cycles.

articles.title: Direct effects on gene transcription revealed by global and CRISPR-targeted oxidative DNA damage
articles.abstract: Oxidative stress induces rapid expression changes of specific genes. However, whether these changes are due to direct and local DNA oxidation and whether they depend on the repair machinery is still debated. Here, we show by total RNA-Seq that upon oxidative stress, many genes are either rapidly repressed or activated. The early transcriptional response also includes the activation of many read-through RNAs. Importantly, degradation of the endogenous OGG1 DNA glycosylase showed that the early repression of these genes partially depends on OGG1, therefore demonstrating that these genome expression changes are due to the processing of oxidized DNA. We further demonstrate by ChIPseq against total or S5-phosphorylated RNA polymerase II that transcriptional regulation by oxidative stress involves changes in the recruitment of RNA polymerase II to transcription start sites. Finally, through the use of a chemoptogenetic system allowing the targeting of ROS to chosen genomic loci, we were able to reproduce repression of some genes through the local induction of oxidative DNA damage at their promoters, demonstrating that local DNA oxidation directly affects transcription of genes. Altogether, our results show that local oxidative DNA damage leads to alterations in the activity of specific promoters by a mechanism dependent on repair processes.

articles.title: Disease-associated NK-cell state remodeling reveals transcriptional profiles predictive of clinical phenotypes
articles.abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells adapt their cellular states to diverse tissue and inflammatory environments, yet how this plasticity manifests across pathological contexts and relates to patient-level disease phenotypes remains poorly defined. Here we established the Human NK-cell Atlas (HNKA) from over 1 million NK cells, including samples from 1,632 donors spanning 50 diseases. Within a shared NK-cell state architecture, analyses of state abundance and matched-reference exceedance distinguished disease-biased redistribution from transcriptional displacement. Fine-grained analyses localized disease-associated remodeling to specific NK-cell states, including CD56dim NK ISG15 in infection and autoimmunity and CD56bright NK ITM2C in tumors. These patterns were accompanied by recurrent interferon responses and state-specific regulatory activity. Cytokine perturbations recapitulated key transcriptional features of disease-associated NK-cell states. We developed NKceiver, a model based on state-specific NK-cell expression profiles for patient-level prediction. It distinguished 18 diseases and predicted COVID-19 severity and response to immune checkpoint inhibitors, with predictive performance retained in unseen patients and studies. Collectively, our results reveal that disease-associated remodeling within the diverse NK-cell state repertoire resolved by HNKA is biologically interpretable and clinically informative, supporting disease discrimination and prediction of clinical phenotypes.

articles.title: Dissociable episodic memory performance and subjective experience across the aphantasia imagery spectrum
articles.abstract: Mental imagery is often assumed to support episodic memory, yet whether this relationship depends on conscious access to imagery, and how reduced imagery differs from total aphantasia, remains unclear. The present study compared objective episodic memory performance, subjective trial-by-trial vividness, confidence, and response times in people reporting normal imagery, reduced imagery, or total aphantasia, across younger and older age groups. Participants completed an incidental-encoding episodic memory task requiring identification of visual or spatial changes in targets within scenes, alongside trial-by-trial vividness and confidence ratings. Across the full imagery spectrum, trial-level fluctuations in vividness were related to memory performance, whereas trait-level and averaged vividness measures were not. Moreover, reduced imagery and total aphantasia showed dissociable patterns of episodic memory performance and subjective experience. In the reduced-imagery group, vividness was a stronger predictor of accuracy and response times, vividness judgements were slower, and confidence was lower, suggesting greater metacognitive uncertainty when imagery is weak and inconsistent. Controls outperformed reduced and aphantasic groups on visual but not spatial changes, and both groups responded more slowly than controls; confidence did not differ between control and aphantasic groups. Age-related memory decline was observed in the control and reduced groups but not in the aphantasic group. Exit questionnaire data highlighted limited awareness of aphantasia among typical imagers and a persistent belief among aphantasic participants that their memory was inferior. Together, these findings show that reduced imagery should be distinguished from total aphantasia rather than treating both as a single population, and that trial-level fluctuations in vividness reveal relationships with episodic memory that trait-level and averaged measures do not capture.

articles.title: Divide and conquer: a viral bifunctional RNA utilizes both RNA and protein to modulate pro-tumourigenic pathways
articles.abstract: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is an oncogenic herpesvirus that causes the endothelial cell neoplasm Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) and other B-cell malignancies. The viral transcript kaposin is largely composed of GC-rich direct repeats (DRs) and is expressed during all phases of KSHV replication. Kaposin is polycistronic, encoding for at least 3 kaposin (Kap) proteins; of these, KapB is the most abundant and well-studied. Recent work from our lab discovered that kaposin is found in nuclear speckles (NSs) and that DRs are required for NS retention. During latency, kaposin is predominantly in NSs and is not exported or translated into KapB. During viral reactivation, abundant kaposin correlates with kaposin escape from NSs and KapB protein production. Thus, although kaposin is a latent transcript, KapB protein production occurs only during lytic reactivation. The spatiotemporal regulation of kaposin translation by NS retention during KSHV latency likewise suggests that these two biomolecules may have distinct functions. Because historically kaposin was viewed as a protein-coding mRNA, overexpression studies attributed any function to KapB even though both kaposin and KapB were produced in these systems. Armed with the knowledge that kaposin is a bifunctional RNA which derives function from both the transcript and the protein(s) it encodes, it remains unclear whether prior phenotypes should be attributed to kaposin or KapB. In this study, we developed a reductionist overexpression system to uncouple the effects of these biomolecules. To mimic kaposin during viral latency, we used a construct capable of forming kaposin NSs that does not translate reported Kap proteins ({Delta}Starts). To mimic late lytic reactivation, we used a recoded construct, AltB, that does not form kaposin NSs, is readily exported from the nucleus, and translates abundant KapB. We found that KapB protein induced actin stress fibre formation, cell enlargement, increased total levels of Yes-associated protein (YAP) and increased YAP-target gene transcription including pro-growth and pro-inflammatory transcripts. Conversely, kaposin RNA induced cell autonomous p-body disassembly with an overall reduction in pro-growth and pro-inflammatory transcripts, suggesting kaposin might sustain cell survival while dampening immune signalling. Taken together, we demonstrate that kaposin RNA and KapB protein have distinct and sometimes opposing effects on cellular growth and inflammatory signalling pathways, highlighting the ability of a viral bifunctional RNA to use both its RNA and protein products to mediate viral tumourigenesis.

articles.title: Drag racers and long haulers: the design space of myosin-V-like motor proteins
articles.abstract: The ubiquitous myosin class-V molecular motors transport cellular cargo long distances at roughly 0.5 μm/s. Plant-specific myosin class-XI motors share nearly identical structural features with myosin-V, yet display velocities from 0.25 to 70 μm/s, the fastest transport motor in nature. Empirical observations suggest an inverse relationship between run length and velocity. These observations raise a central question: how can a single motor design support both highly processive "long-hauler" and extremely rapid "drag-racer" motors? We generalize a polymer-based model of force-dependent myosin-V dynamics to encompass the broader design space. The model quantitatively captures experimental data from fast myosin-XI and yields general analytical expressions for key observables. Notably, we derive a Pareto frontier that defines the trade-off between velocity and run distance, as well as the theoretical maximum velocity achievable by such motors. Our results establish the biological limits of natural and synthetic myosin-V-like motor design.

articles.title: Enhancing working memories using repetitive TMS
articles.abstract: Working memory, the ability to retain and manipulate information no longer present in the environment, is fundamental for goal-directed behavior (Baddeley, 2012; Baddeley & Hitch, 1974; D'Esposito, 2007; D'Esposito & Postle, 2015). Alpha oscillations (~8-12 Hz) have two apparently contradictory roles in working memory. Alpha activity gates irrelevant information through inhibition, a role causally supported by rhythmic transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of parietal cortex at alpha frequency when a retrospective cue renders a memory item irrelevant (Bonnefond & Jensen, 2012; Riddle et al., 2020). Yet alpha activity also tracks the content of memory and binds the features of memorized objects during maintenance (Foster et al., 2016; Pagnotta et al., 2026). Whether alpha oscillations causally support the fidelity of memory representations during maintenance is untested. Here, 24 participants received short trains of repetitive TMS (rTMS) at theta (6 Hz) or alpha frequency (10 Hz), or in an arrhythmic control pattern, during the second half of the delay of a color working memory task, over the left posterior inferior frontal sulcus or the left intraparietal sulcus. A mixture model separated memory precision from swap errors and guesses. Alpha stimulation of the intraparietal sulcus specifically increased memory precision, whereas rhythmic stimulation of either site reduced response error, guesses and swaps irrespective of frequency. These results provide causal evidence that alpha oscillations support the fidelity of working memory representations during maintenance, and show that rhythmic stimulation at the appropriate frequency, site and time can enhance human working memory. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.

articles.title: Excluded Volume Effect-induced Shrinkage for Resolution Enhancement of Hydrogel Bioconstructs
articles.abstract: Biofabrication of hydrogel materials is usually constrained by process-specific resolution limits. Here, we introduce excluded volume effect-induced shrinkage (EVER), a dehydration-enabled resolution enhancement strategy that achieves dimensional refinement via post-processing. In this approach, we treat biofabricated constructs with hydrophilic macromolecular crowding agent bath, with poloxamer as a representative. With EVER treatment, gelatin-based constructs can reach a dimension reduction of up to ~49% with an estimated volumetric reduction of ~87%. Shape fidelity was well retained after shrinkage across different constructs and could be stabilized by introducing secondary crosslinking. In extrusion bioprinted cell-laden constructs, myoblasts retained a considerable cell viability right after the shrinkage treatment and recovered significantly by day 1, with subsequent cell spreading and increasing proliferation over 7 days. Without the need of continued immersion in the shrinkage bath, EVER provides a hardware-independent route for refining hydrogel structures while retaining encapsulated cell compatibility.

articles.title: Fine-tuning an intracellular allosteric pocket programs GPCR signaling bias
articles.abstract: Biased signaling of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) offers a route for precise therapeutics with fewer adverse effects. Intracellular allosteric ligands can impose such bias, yet how subtle chemical changes within these pockets reshape receptor-transducer coupling and downstream signaling remains unclear. Here, we systematically fine-tuned the intracellular allosteric pocket of neurotensin receptor 1 (NTSR1) through chemical modification of the β-arrestin-biased ligand SBI-553. Minor changes to the ligand scaffold altered transducer-coupling preferences, generating distinct profiles of G-protein and β-arrestin signaling. Cryo-electron microscopy structures of NTSR1-β-arrestin2 complexes bound to designed allosteric probes revealed ligand-dependent remodeling of the intracellular cavity that reshapes the receptor-effector interface. Alanine scanning identified transducer-sensitive residues within and beyond the immediate ligand-contact region. In mice, SBI-553 and N065 produced distinct physiological profiles, with N065 improving survival in a lethal endotoxemia model. Finally, phosphoproteomic profiling revealed partially overlapping but distinct downstream signaling profiles among the three modulators. Together, these findings establish the intracellular allosteric pocket as a tunable determinant of transducer coupling and show that closely related modulators can generate distinct signaling and physiological profiles. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. Innovative Drug Research and Development National Science and Technology Major Project, 2025ZD1803100, 2025ZD1803104 Shanghai Municipal Health Commission, 2025ZHYL038 Lingang Laboratory, LG8888 National Natural Science Foundation of China, 82441035, 22237005, 824B2105, 82504673, 32130022, 82495184 National Key R&D Program of China, 2023YFC3605500, 2022YFC2703105, 2022YFE0203600, 2024YFA1307504 Zhongshan Municipal Bureau of Science and Technology, CXTD2023010 CAS Strategic Priority Research Program, XDB37030103 Shanghai Municipal Science and Technology Major Project, 2019SHZDZX02 The HE Research Fellowship, HERF2025011 Shanghai Leading Talent Program of Eastern Talent Plan, QNKJ2025058 The Innovative Research Team of High-Level Local Universities in Shanghai

articles.title: Focal neuronal loss and cell replacement in a connectome model of fly steering
articles.abstract: Focal neuronal loss after stroke, traumatic brain injury or spinal cord injury can disrupt circuits and result in persistent motor deficits. Which cells and connections must be restored to recover a specific behavior is difficult to establish experimentally. Here we use a connectome-constrained spiking model of the fruit-fly nervous system and decode motor-neuron output to simulate visually guided steering. After loss of 4,000 neurons, path straightness ranged from 0.04 to 0.95 depending on lesion location. At a fixed sensorimotor site, a 2,000-neuron lesion reduced simulated displacement to 6.5% of intact. Across 100 stochastic simulation realizations of the connectome, replacing 100 cells with their original connections increased displacement to 62.5% of intact when motor-control pathways were prioritized, compared with 10.1% after random selection of 100 cells and 48.5% after random selection of 1,000 cells. When connections were instead inferred from cell type, the same 100 intended replacements reached 60.0% of intact with matched identities and 6.7% with non-target identities, indicating that cell identity and type-dependent integration are required for recovery. Our model generates testable predictions for genetic ablation experiments in fruit flies and identifies candidate cellular and circuit requirements for motor repair that can inform cell replacement therapies and future models of mammalian locomotion.

articles.title: GLOM TGITO: multiscale protein modelling and multiview landscape-guided sequence discovery
articles.abstract: Motivation: Offline protein design can exploit surrogate-predictor errors, favouring high-scoring sequences lacking measured support. We test whether multiscale representations and local experimental evidence improve prediction and candidate prioritization. Results: GLOM-TGITO links a global-local fluorescence predictor to multiview landscape-guided optimization. Across 31,434 measured ppluGFP2 sequences, GLOM achieved random/depth-holdout RMSEs of 0.170/0.247 versus 0.247/0.324 for the strongest SaProt-650M controls. Averaged across three training seeds, 96.3%/97.3% of prediction-ranked Top 100 test variants were measured bright (log10 fluorescence >=4.2). Search from 900 peak regions yielded 2,594 distinct candidate sequences. The selected Top 100 showed 2.9-8.2% lower mean representation deviation than four comparator pipelines; 38 versus 11-16 met joint novelty-reliability filters. Deviation identified measured test errors >0.1 (AUROC

articles.title: Genome-Wide Transcriptomics Uncovers a Lung-to-Aorta Inflammatory Program Driving Influenza-Induced Atherosclerosis Exacerbation
articles.abstract: Influenza infection increases cardiovascular risk in individuals with pre-existing atherosclerosis, yet the genome-wide transcriptional basis of this association remains undefined. We performed bulk RNA sequencing of aorta and lung tissues from high-fat diet-fed Apoe-/- mice infected with influenza A/PR/8/34 versus PBS-treated controls at day 15 post-infection, identifying 6,828 differentially expressed genes across both tissues (5,694 in the lung and 1,134 in the aorta; adjusted p < 0.05). In the lung, influenza sustained a CXCR3-driven chemokine storm, comprehensive Th1, Th17, and exhaustion T-cell activation programs, coordinated monocyte recruitment through Ccl2, Ccl7, Ccl8, and Ccl12, a broad acute phase response including Saa3 and A2m, alveolar identity collapse through loss of Nkx2-1 and surfactant proteins, and broad metabolic dysregulation involving suppression of fatty acid oxidation, mitochondrial function, and circadian metabolic regulators. In the aorta, influenza drove macrophage and DAMP activation through Trem1, Fpr2, and S100a8, cytotoxic T-cell engagement, smooth muscle cell dedifferentiation through Myocd loss, convergent bioenergetic failure, and an ectopic lung-identity gene signature representing a previously undescribed cross-organ communication mechanism. Circadian clock and Hippo/YAP pathway suppression were shared across both tissues, identifying systemic vulnerabilities connecting pulmonary infection to vascular structural compromise. Consistent with the in vivo findings, influenza-infected Apoe-/- bone marrow-derived macrophages exhibited inflammasome activation, DAMP amplification, M1 polarization, and suppression of prostaglandin-mediated inflammatory resolution. Together these findings define a lung-to-aorta inflammatory and metabolic axis driving atherosclerotic plaque destabilization during the post-infection recovery period and identify CCR2/CXCR3 antagonism, NLRP3 inhibition, and YAP pathway activation as candidate therapeutic interventions.

articles.title: Glycogen removal enhances ethylene production in Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 but exposes a 2-oxoglutarate-GS-GOGAT-phosphate constraint
articles.abstract: Cyanobacteria are promising platforms for converting CO2 directly into value-added chemicals. However, redirecting fixed carbon toward a product requires understanding of how cells balance the energetic and redox supplies and demands - and how efficiently metabolic flux can be channelled into product formation rather than being dissipated or excreted. Glycogen, synthesized via ADP-glucose pyrophosphorylase (GlgC), is the major native carbon and energy sink, and its removal forces cells to redirect excess carbon and reducing power into alternative pathways. As a target product we used ethylene, a major industrial building block currently derived almost entirely from fossil feedstocks, which can be produced photoautotrophically by the ethylene-forming enzyme (EFE) at the expense of 2-oxoglutarate (2-OG), a central node linking carbon and nitrogen metabolism. Here, we compared wild-type Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 with strains carrying either a complete ({Delta}glgC) or attenuated, light-responsive (LGS; psbA2-driven glgC) glycogen synthesis block, with an EFE-expressing strain (EFE), and with the combined {Delta}glgC+EFE strain. All strains were cultivated across a light gradient (35-300 mol photons m-2 s-1) under nitrogen-replete conditions. Integrating measurements of growth and ethylene production rates, chlorophyll-fluorescence analysis, quantitative proteomics, FTIR profiling, and overflow-metabolite analysis revealed that partial suppression of glycogen synthesis (LGS) enhanced growth under low irradiance but became detrimental above a critical light threshold. EFE expression in the {Delta}glgC background increased ethylene production in a light-dependent manner but further compromised growth. Both strains with EFE increased photosynthetic electron transport consistent with the carbon-sink effect, yet this electron surplus was not channelled proportionally into product or biomass. Instead, continuous 2-OG drain by EFE constrained flux through the GS-GOGAT node and induced a secondary inorganic phosphate limitation in {Delta}glgC+EFE that activated photoprotection and limited productivity. These results point to the 2-OG/GS-GOGAT/Pi axis as a key design constraint determining whether the surplus photosynthetic flux gets converted into product, dissipated through photoprotection, or released as overflow metabolites.

articles.title: Hepatocyte nuclear factor-1β recruits the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase complex to activate gene transcription
articles.abstract: Mutations affecting the transcription factor hepatocyte nuclear factor-1β (HNF-1β) are the most common monogenic cause of congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract. The mechanism whereby HNF-1β regulates gene transcription remains unclear. Here, we performed an unbiased proteomic screen and found that endogenous HNF-1β interacts with core subunits of the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase complex (NuRD) in renal epithelial cells. Genome-wide ChIP-seq studies demonstrated colocalization of endogenous HNF-1β and the core NuRD subunits GATAD2A, CHD4, and MBD3 at 2,776 primarily intergenic and intronic sites in native chromatin from wild-type renal epithelial cells. NuRD co-occupancy at 628 of the sites (22.6%) was reduced in the absence of HNF-1β. Of the 628 HNF-1β-dependent NuRD-occupied sites, 113 sites (18.2%) showed higher ATAC-seq peaks, indicative of open chromatin, and enrichment of histone H3 lysine-27 (H3K27) acetylation, indicative of active enhancers, in wild-type cells compared to HNF-1β-deficient cells. Correlation with transcriptomic profiles in wild-type and HNF-1β-deficient cells revealed that most of the sites were located near genes that are activated by HNF-1β. Knockdown of CHD4 with shRNA resulted in decreased expression of 67 HNF-1β-regulated genes that contained nearby NuRD and HNF-1β co-occupied sites. Collectively, these results demonstrate that HNF-1β recruits the NuRD complex resulting in H3K27 acetylation and chromatin opening and leading to gene activation. Our findings reveal a new mechanism of HNF-1β-dependent gene expression and expand the role of the NuRD complex in gene activation at distal enhancers. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. NIH, R01 DK042921, R01 HD120295, S10OD028717

articles.title: High-content imaging of live microglia-containing Alzheimer's disease brain organoids
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common progressive neurodegenerative disease for which there is currently no safe and effective treatment. AD is characterized by the pathological aggregation of amyloid-β (Aβ) in the brain resulting in neuronal dysfunction/death and cognitive decline. Modeling these processes in vitro remains challenging due to the lack of an immune-competent 3D in vitro human model of AD amenable to high-throughput analyses. Conventional cerebral organoids (COs) lack microglia and are optically dense which precludes real-time longitudinal analyses. Here, we employ the fluorescent amyloid probe PyrPeg to selectively monitor Aβ aggregation, and calcein AM and propidium iodide to assess cellular viability within microglia-containing COs (MCOs). We identify age-dependent DS-AD-associated phenotypes within T21 MCOs including Aβ neuropathology, neurodegeneration, and glial cell dysregulation. Our platform supports real-time, multiplexed tracking of disease progression and provides a scalable platform for longitudinal analyses studying disease mechanisms and targeted approaches to treatment. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. National Institute on Aging, https://ror.org/049v75w11, R01AG078965, RF1AG078965

articles.title: How Much Can AI Virtual Cells Gain from Unified Perturbational Modeling?
articles.abstract: Predicting how individual cells respond to perturbations is a central task in artificial intelligence virtual cell (AIVC) modeling. However, integrating perturbation datasets is challenging because they differ in measured gene sets, perturbation types and cellular contexts. Existing AIVC predictors are typically developed for specific settings, limiting their applicability across heterogeneous datasets. Here, we investigate the extent to which AIVC predictors can benefit from unified perturbational modeling (UPM), a novel paradigm designed to integrate heterogeneous Perturb-seq datasets into a single predictive model. To this end, we introduce three unification modules into a variational autoencoder (VAE)-based AIVC predictor to address these sources of heterogeneity: gene-channel alignment, shared perturbation encoding, and joint embedding of gene expression and identity. We systematically evaluate and validate the individual contributions of these modules. Building on UPM, we assemble a dataset of 110 million cells spanning over 22,000 genes, four perturbation types and 76 cellular contexts, and use 89.7 million cells from 71 contexts to train a unified AIVC predictor with more than one billion parameters. Across genetic perturbation benchmarks, UPM achieves the highest PES and gene-wise response correlation among the evaluated models. It also improves all four evaluation metrics over State on the five held-out Tahoe-100M cell lines and over Stack on the cytokine benchmark. UPM also improves combinatorial perturbation prediction relative to specialized predictors. In the HSC application, our model achieves a 40.0% improvement in accuracy on a downstream task involving the recapitulation of effects induced by the knockdown of hepatic stellate cell (HSC)-related targets. Our implementation is openly available at https://github.com/youlab2025/UPM.

articles.title: Human prion proteins and mutants through the lens of systems biology
articles.abstract: Autocatalytic conformational changes of cellular prion proteins (PrP C ) to the β-sheet-enriched scrapie isoform (PrP SC ) drive prion diseases, yet the precise molecular mechanisms remain unclear. To address this, we employ a multi-pronged framework integrating network-theoretic analyses, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and experimental validation to characterize critical residues governing human PrP (huPrP) structural integrity. Residue Interaction Networks (RINs) of: (A) wild-type (WT) huPrP, and, (B) five disease-associated point mutants (Met166Val, Glu220Lys, Glu200Lys, Asp178Asn, and Ser170Asn) were evaluated using three rigorous network methods: centrality measures, S hortest P ath A lteration F raction (SPAF), and D ifferential N etworks (DN). Across all the diverse point mutations, five residues (Met206, Val209, Val210, Met213, and Cys214) consistently exhibit high centrality scores. SPAF and DN analyses demonstrate that alterations at these positions disrupt connectivity and increase the propensity for misfolding and protease resistance. To validate these topological findings, key residues within the C-terminal domain (121-230) were substituted via site-directed mutagenesis. Thermal denaturation monitored by circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy reveals that the Met213Ala substitution significantly lowers the melting temperature, T m , relative to the WT, whereas the Val210Ala variant unfolds with a T m comparable to the WT. Furthermore, MD simulations of de novo AlphaFold-predicted mutant structures corroborate these findings. Mutants exhibit greater structural flexibility and deviation, with average root Mean Square Deviations rising from 0.18 nm (WT) to 0.32 nm (Cys214Ala), 0.29 nm (Met206Ala), and 0.25 nm (Val210Lys). This integration of theoretical and experimental techniques provides a robust framework for identifying critical determinants of protein stability.

articles.title: IL-27 Reduces Cell-Surface LDLR in Human Macrophages and Restricts VSV-G-Pseudotyped HIV infection
articles.abstract: Low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) is a major cellular receptor for vesicular stomatitis virus glycoprotein (VSV-G), which is widely used to pseudo-type viral vectors. We previously showed that IL-27 suppresses infection by VSV-G-pseudotyped HIV encoding luciferase (VSV-G-HIVLuc) in macrophages; although IL-27 induced multiple anti-virus genes in cell, the underlying mechanism of VSVG-HIVLuc inhibition remains poorly understood. Here, we examined whether IL-27 regulates LDLR expression and contributes to suppression of VSV-G-HIVLuc infection. Monocyte-derived macrophages differentiated with M-CSF or GM-CSF, with or without IL-27, were analyzed for cell-surface LDLR by flow cytometry, LDLR transcripts by quantitative RT-PCR, and total LDLR protein by Western blotting. Viral binding, proviral DNA, and reporter expression were evaluated by cell-associated p24 antigen, late reverse-transcription products, and luciferase activity, respectively. IL-27 reduced surface LDLR to 38.3 {+/-} 2.6 % in M-CSF-derived macrophages (p<0.01) and 31.4{+/-} 3.2 % in GM-CSF-derived macrophages (p<0.01). Western Blotting demonstrated that total LDLR protein decreased to 48 {+/-} 0.8 % in IL-27-treated M-CSF-derived macrophages (27M-Mac) (p<0.01) while it was not significantly changed in IL-27-treated GM-CSF-derived macrophages (27GM-Mac), although approximately 1.6~1.9-fold increase in LDLR transcripts following IL-27 treatment in both macrophages (p<0.01). Viral binding decreased to nearly 50 % in 27GM but not significantly changed on 27M-Mac whereas late reverse-transcription products decreased to 23 {+/-} 2.1% (p<0.0001) and 44 {+/-} 1.5% (p<0.0001). Luciferase activity was further reduced to 5.8 {+/-} 0.4 % and 5.9 {+/-} 2.1 % (both p<0.0001). These findings demonstrate that IL-27 downregulates cell-surface LDLR in human macrophages, suggesting that IL-27 restricts VSV-G-pseudo-typed Lenti virus infection through both receptor-associated and additional post-entry mechanisms.

articles.title: Inferring somatic copy number aberrations from spatial transcriptomics data to study early cancer development
articles.abstract: Understanding the spatial organisation of cells undergoing early transformation and their interactions with the local microenvironment is critical to studying the earliest stages of cancer development. Somatic copy number aberrations (SCNAs) are among the earliest genomic alterations observed in many cancers, but their spatial context remains difficult to study using conventional sequencing approaches. We developed a computational framework to infer SCNAs directly from Xenium spatial transcriptomics data, enabling the identification and spatial mapping of cell populations sharing common SCNA profiles. Applying this approach to ovarian, cervical and breast cancer datasets identified spatially coherent SCNA-defined populations that recapitulated known tumour-associated copy number aberrations and pathological states. In high-grade serous ovarian cancer, we identified an intermediate epithelial population within the fallopian tube exhibiting features of early transformation accompanied by immune remodelling. Together, our pipeline establishes a scalable framework for reconstructing the spatial architecture of SCNA-defined clones, providing new opportunities to identify and characterise candidate early transforming cell populations in situ. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. CRUK, ACEPGM-2023/100001, SEBCD3-2024/100001 NIHR UCLH Biomedical Research Centre, BRC1113/CN/FM/101330 NIHR Cambridge Biomedical Research Centre, NIHR203312

articles.title: Information coding strategies in biological reservoir computing for multiclass time-series classification
articles.abstract: Physical reservoir computing (RC) using biological neural networks (BNNs) offers a framework for probing how high-dimensional dynamics arising from multicellular systems support complex information processing in the brain. However, how electrical inputs and extracellular readouts should be designed to suit different task demands remains unclear. Here, using primary rat cortical neurons cultured on a high-density microelectrode array, we investigated how input encoding and spike detection methods influence neural representations and the resulting RC performance in BNNs. Comparison of pulse amplitude modulation and latency coding revealed that the latter exhibited superior performance in demanding multiclass conditions, including a 10% improvement in a 10-class spoken digit classification task. Spike sorting further improved classification performance by enhancing class separability, while largely preserving the low-dimensional structure of population activity. These findings highlight the importance of designing information coding strategies according to task difficulty.

articles.title: Integrative Single-Cell Transcriptomics and Explainable AI for Disease Mechanism and Biomarker Discovery in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
articles.abstract: Invasion is an early step in the metastatic spread of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), yet cells within a single tumour or cell line differ in their capacity to invade, and it is unclear which transcriptional features distinguish cells that invade from those that do not. We re-analysed the public single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset GSE329526, in which ClonMapper-barcoded MDA-MB-231 cells were separated in a transwell assay into invasive (five samples, 6,289 cells) and non-invasive (five samples, 5,983 cells) fractions and compared with the parental population (one sample, 3,022 cells). An initial cell-level analysis combined Wilcoxon differential expression, an XGBoost classifier with a random cell split, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Enrichr over-representation analysis. Because cells from the same sample are not independent, we then repeated the analysis at the sample level, using differential expression on sample means (five versus five), XGBoost with cross-validation that held out whole samples, a quality-control-metric baseline model, SHAP on held-out samples and rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA). At the sample level, 6,651 of 11,727 tested genes differed between invasive and non-invasive samples (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05), including the ten top-ranked cell-level genes such as PHLDA2, ANTXR2, VIM and HMGA1 (FDR 0.0007 to 0.0022) and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) regulators TGFBR2, JAG1, SDCBP and WWTR1. With whole samples held out, XGBoost distinguished invasive from non-invasive cells with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.92 (range across folds 0.89 to 0.95); removing ribosomal and mitochondrial genes did not change performance (AUC 0.92), whereas a model using only four quality-control metrics reached 0.63, and every held-out invasive sample received a higher mean predicted probability of invasion (0.74 to 0.79) than every non-invasive sample (0.20 to 0.28). On held-out samples, SHAP ranked inflammatory and stress-response genes highest (CCL2, LGALS12, DUSP1, CXCL3, KYNU, CXCL2), and GSEA showed higher KRAS signalling (normalised enrichment score [NES] 2.30, FDR 0.001) and E2F targets (NES 1.62, FDR 0.038) and lower interferon-alpha and interferon-gamma responses (NES -1.97 and -1.65; FDR 0.001 and 0.019) in invasive samples. The ribosomal genes that dominated the original SHAP ranking were absent from the held-out ranking. Invasive MDA-MB-231 cells therefore carry a transcriptional state that is reproducible across independent transwell samples and involves EMT-related, inflammatory and proliferative programmes. Limitations include a single cell line, sequencing of the invasive and non-invasive populations in separate libraries and the absence of external validation; the candidate genes reported here are hypotheses that require confirmation in independent experiments and patient material.

articles.title: Isocaloric restriction normalizes body weight but not relative adiposity, adipose inflammation, or gut microbial diversity in high-fat diet-fed mice
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: The separate contributions of excess energy intake and diet composition to high-fat diet (HFD)-induced adiposity, adipose inflammation, and gut microbial changes are unclear. We tested whether restricting HFD intake to the energy intake of low-fat (LF)-fed mice (isocaloric restriction) prevents or reverses these outcomes. Subjects/Methods: Male C57BL/6 mice (n = 8/group) received for 12 weeks an LF diet (LF/LF) or HFD (HF/HF) ad libitum, HFD ad libitum then isocaloric HFD from week 7 (HF/IHF), or isocaloric HFD throughout (IHF/IHF). Adiposity, plasma markers, adipose and ileal gene expression, and fecal microbiota (16S rRNA sequencing, n = 4/group) were assessed. Results: Final body weight in IHF/IHF did not differ from LF/LF (difference 0.1 g, 95% CI -6.5 to 6.7; P > 0.99) and was lower than in HF/HF (-8.2 g, -14.7 to -1.6; P = 0.011). Switching to isocaloric feeding reduced weight gain during weeks 6-12 (HF/IHF vs HF/HF, -6.4 g, -9.8 to -3.1; P < 0.001). IHF/IHF mice had lower glucose (P = 0.031) and cholesterol (P = 0.005) than HF/HF mice. However, visceral fat relative to body weight remained higher than in LF/LF in IHF/IHF (+1.5 percentage points, 0.04 to 2.9; P = 0.042) and HF/IHF (+1.8, 0.4 to 3.3; P = 0.008). Adipose Tnf expression remained elevated in HF/IHF (log2 difference 2.2, 0.2 to 4.2; P = 0.025), and fecal phylogenetic diversity was lower in IHF/IHF than in LF/LF (Faith's PD -3.1, -5.9 to -0.4; P = 0.024). Ileal barrier genes and plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein were unchanged. Conclusions: Limiting HFD energy intake normalized body weight, glycemia, and plasma lipids but not relative adiposity, adipose Tnf expression, or the loss of gut microbial diversity. Diet composition affects these outcomes independently of energy intake, so normal body weight does not indicate their reversal. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) grants funded by the Korea government (MSIT), NRF-2022R1F1A1060025, RS-2025-00521084

articles.title: Lateral-eyed tree shrews combine panoramic vision with an expanded oculomotor repertoire
articles.abstract: Mammals differ in how they redirect gaze. Primates shift and hold gaze with rapid, precise eye movements that can be decoupled from the head. In lateral-eyed mammals studied to date, gaze is organized around the head: saccades are coupled to head rotation in freely moving animals and typically accompanied by attempted head movements even under head fixation. These observations suggest a trade-off: animals that keep a panoramic field give up the precise, eye-driven control of gaze typical of frontal-eyed animals. But because lateral eyes and head-centered gaze co-occur in every lateral-eyed species studied, it is unknown whether one follows from the other. Here we test this in the tree shrew, an arboreal mammal with laterally placed eyes. Using real-time eye tracking in head-fixed animals, we find that tree shrews saccade frequently under head fixation and that most saccades occur without detectable attempted head movement. Tree shrews make visually evoked saccades, along both the horizontal and vertical axes of the visual field, toward targets. They can also fixate on visual targets. Using widefield calcium imaging, we show that visual cortex over-represents the central visual field. Lastly, we show that extraocular muscles contain morphologically elaborate palisade endings, specialized nerve endings that are a constant feature of frontal-eyed species. Lateral eyes therefore do not preclude eye-driven gaze control. The two are separable dimensions of visual system design, a combination that may suit animals whose locomotion routinely points the head away from where they need to look.

articles.title: Long-term experimental evolution of seasonal influenza A/H3N2 virus reveals diverse evolutionary potential
articles.abstract: The repeatability of evolutionary outcomes is a fundamental question with implications for predicting the evolution pathogens like influenza viruses. Here, we tested whether seasonal A/H3N2 influenza virus evolution follows reproducible paths in a simplified setting where the natural cellular environment is maintained but adaptive immune selection is removed. We serially passaged replicate populations of an A/H3N2 virus for 1,200 generations across 12 independent differentiated human airway epithelium culture lines (three replicates of four donors) and performed deep sequencing to reconstruct the evolutionary dynamics. Rates of variant accumulation differed significantly among lines but not among donors, and parallel evolution was minimal. Populations generated polymorphisms not observed in the global human population, reversions to historical sequences, and changes at positions held near-invariant globally since 1968. These findings suggest A/H3N2 evolutionary trajectories are shaped less by intrinsic functional constraint than by selective context and help explain why predicting influenza virus evolution remains difficult.

articles.title: Lymphoma response to chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy is driven by endogenous tumor-reactive CD8⁺ T cells
articles.abstract: CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy induces durable remissions in a subset of patients with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma; however, most patients fail to respond or eventually relapse. By integrating whole-genome and transcriptome profiling of 54 patients with functional assays, syngeneic models, and mathematical modeling, we demonstrate that durable CAR-T efficacy requires cooperation between CAR-T cells and endogenous CD8⁺ (eCD8) T cells recruited to join the attack on malignant cells. Tumors with biallelic loss of MHC class I or CD58 exhibited high genomic complexity, increased neoantigen burden, and resistance to CAR-T therapy. MHC-I-deficient lymphomas showed suboptimal response in immunocompetent hosts compared to wild type. Importantly, sustained responses in mice occurred only in the presence of eCD8 cells, whereas all CD8⁺-depleted mice relapsed after initial CAR-T-mediated tumor regression. Patients and murine ELISPOT assays confirmed enhanced endogenous T-cell activation post-CAR-T. These findings reveal that CAR-T therapy functions not only as a cytotoxic modality but also as a catalyst for endogenous anti-tumor immunity. ### Competing Interest Statement O.L. has received research funding from: National Institutes of Health (NIH), National Cancer Institute (NCI), U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Multiple Myeloma Research Foundation (MMRF), International Myeloma Foundation (IMF), Leukemia and Lymphoma Society (LLS), Myeloma Solutions Fund (MSF), Paula and Rodger Riney Multiple Myeloma Research Program Fund, the Tow Foundation, Perelman Family Foundation, Rising Tide Foundation, Amgen, Celgene, Janssen, Takeda, Glenmark, Seattle Genetics, Karyopharm; Honoraria/ad boards: Adaptive, Amgen, Binding Site, BMS, Celgene, Cellectis, Glenmark, Janssen, Juno, Pfizer; and serves on Independent Data Monitoring Committees (IDMCs) for clinical trials lead by Takeda, Merck, Janssen, Theradex. articles.title: MPFIL: Multi-Level Protein Feature Integration for Predicting Mutation-Induced Protein-Protein Binding Affinity Changes
articles.abstract: Predicting mutation-induced changes in protein protein binding affinity ({triangleup}{triangleup}G) is challenging because mutations can affect both local residue environments and the structural organization of protein complexes. Existing approaches often rely on handcrafted physicochemical, energetic, or evolutionary features, which introduce additional computational costs and require domain-specific knowledge. In this work, we propose MPFIL, a multi-level protein feature integration framework for predicting mutation-induced protein-protein binding affin ity changes. MPFIL integrates structural and sequential infor mation to characterize mutation effects from complementary perspectives. Its structural feature extraction module captures mutation-induced structural changes and differential information between wild-type and mutant complexes, while sequence feature extraction modules model local residue context and long-range dependencies. The resulting features are integrated for {triangleup}{triangleup}G prediction. We evaluate MPFIL on three benchmark datasets. Experimental results demonstrate competitive and consistent performance across different protein complex settings, while ablation studies verify the contribution of the structural and sequential features. These results support the effectiveness of multi-level protein feature integration for modeling mutation induced changes in protein-protein binding affinity.

articles.title: A GCN1-independent activator of the kinase GCN2
articles.abstract: Mutations of EIF2AK4, which encodes the eIF2α kinase GCN2, cause a severe inherited form of pulmonary hypertension called pulmonary veno-occlusive disease (PVOD). Some pathogenic variants of GCN2 are amenable to pharmacological reactivation by low concentrations of ATP pocket-binding inhibitors. Kinase inhibition at modestly elevated concentrations limits the clinical utility of these drugs against PVOD. We therefore performed an in cellulo chemical screen for GCN2 activators and identified three structurally distinct compounds with low micromolar stimulatory activities. Unlike previously described GCN2 activators, one of these molecules activated GCN2 independently of GCN1. Modelling supported by structure activity screens suggested it binds within the ATP pocket of GCN2, but unlike existing ligands does not protrude inward into the allosteric pocket or outward into the solvent. This overcomes a key requirement of other GCN2 activators.

articles.title: Integration of ATAC- and RNA-sequencing identifies chromatin and transcriptomic signatures in classical and non-classical zebrafish osteoblasts and indicates mechanisms of entpd5a regulation
articles.abstract: Two types of osteoblasts are required to assemble the zebrafish embryonic skeleton: classical osteoblasts homologous to the mammalian cell and notochord sheath cells which serve as non-classical osteoblasts. The gene entpd5a is critically required for ossification via both types of osteoblasts. Despite the indispensability of zebrafish models in vertebrate research, the genetic regulation of bone formation, as well as mechanisms of transcriptional control of entpd5a, remains largely unknown. Here, using a newly generated transgenic line, we isolate classical and non-classical osteoblasts from zebrafish embryos and performed both assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC)-seq and RNA-seq. We analysed results independently and integratively to understand those chromatin dynamics and accompanying transcriptomic changes that occur in different skeletal cell types. We show that although Dlx family factors are playing important roles in classical osteoblast regulation, Hox family factors are involved in governing spinal ossification via non-classical osteoblasts. We further present a resource-driven analysis of the entpd5a promoter, experimentally validating the ATAC-seq dataset and proposing mechanisms of regulating the complex entpd5a expression pattern during zebrafish osteogenesis. Our results thus provide a necessary comprehensive resource for the field of bone development and indicate spatio-temporally regulated promoter/enhancer interactions taking place in the entpd5a locus.

articles.title: Light-entrained chromatin priming poises rapid metamorphosis in a marine sponge
articles.abstract: The most widespread animal life cycle includes a planktonic larval stage that is environmentally induced to settle and rapidly metamorphose into a benthic juvenile. Although this transition is critical for survival, how planetary cues such as light interact with local ecological signals to prepare the genome for such rapid reprogramming remains poorly understood. Here, using the sponge Amphimedon queenslandica, we integrate time-resolved transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility profiling across larval competence, settlement, and the first hours of metamorphosis. We show that diminishing light at sunset is associated with extensive chromatin remodelling in swimming larvae prior to settlement despite relatively modest changes in gene expression. Upon environmental induction by a coralline alga, metamorphosis is accompanied by the rapid and transient activation of a large suite of deeply conserved transcription factors (TFs), including AP-1/bZIP family members, whose binding motifs are enriched in newly accessible regulatory regions near differentially expressed genes. Larvae prevented from experiencing sunset by constant light fail to settle and instead adopt an alternative transcriptional and chromatin state characterised by widespread loss of accessibility and repression of competence-associated TFs, including the circadian regulator CLOCK and other bHLH-PAS factors. These observations support a model in which light-entrained transcriptional activity establishes an anticipatory, permissive chromatin landscape that enables immediate and coordinated transcriptional reprogramming upon environmental induction. We propose that such chromatin priming may represent a broadly deployed regulatory strategy underlying the speed and robustness of metamorphosis in biphasic animal life cycles.

articles.title: Tracking West Nile virus dynamics using viral loads from trapped mosquitoes
articles.abstract: Mosquito-borne virus transmission is increasing globally. Due to a lack of effective vaccines or targeted treatments, mitigation relies on reducing human exposure to infectious mosquitoes. Entomological surveillance provides estimates of human risk by quantifying the prevalence of arboviruses in mosquito populations. Testing of pooled mosquitoes via RT-qPCR is often used to infer infection prevalence; however, these data are often binarised and ignore semi-quantitative cycle threshold (Ct values) that may provide valuable information on virus kinetics, mosquito infectiousness, and ultimately human risk. West Nile virus (WNV) is a globally distributed arbovirus and endemic to the United States. In this study, we analysed pooled Ct values from retrospective mosquito surveillance and found substantial variation that could not be explained by laboratory factors alone. To understand how underlying viral load and epidemiological dynamics might explain this variation, we developed a multi-scale model linking pooled Ct values to heterogeneous within-host viral kinetics in mosquitoes and birds and seasonal transmission dynamics. Our modelling suggests that Ct values from positive pools might reflect a mixture of potentially infectious and non-infectious mosquitoes, indicating that a substantial proportion of PCR-positive mosquitoes might not contribute to transmission. We then developed a method to estimate mosquito infection prevalence using only pooled Ct values that distinguishes infectious from non-infectious prevalence. Estimates of overall prevalence were comparable to standard methods using binarised data and remained accurate at higher prevalences where standard approaches fail. Overall, these findings demonstrate that entomological viral load data reflect biologically meaningful variation in mosquito infection status that is lost through binarisation. Accounting for heterogeneous mosquito viral kinetics can improve interpretation of surveillance data and estimates of transmission risk, with implications for arbovirus surveillance beyond WNV.

articles.title: foxQ2 marks fast-acting interneurons including dopaminergic neurons of mushroom bodies and central complex in the beetle Tribolium castaneum
articles.abstract: The brain is one of the most complex animal organs, and the development of the many different neuron types remains enigmatic. A set of brain-specific transcription factors is involved in brain patterning, but their specific contributions mostly remain to be elucidated, including foxQ2II. This transcription factor is conserved in anterior neuroectodermal patterning of most animals, while it has been lost from vertebrates. The contribution of foxQ2II-positive neurons to the adult brain has remained enigmatic. Here, we use our enhancer trap, immunostainings, and our newly established beetle brainbow system to categorize Tc-foxQ2II-positive neurons into nine clusters with different projection patterns. All clusters contain neurons with the fast-activating neurotransmitters acetylcholine and glutamate, while no Tc-foxQ2II-positive neuron is GABA-ergic or serotonin-positive. Interestingly, we found that many dopaminergic neurons were Tc-foxQ2II positive and homologize them with dopaminergic neurons of the PPL2c, PPM1, and PPL1 cluster described in the Drosophila brain. Our results show that Tc-foxQ2II marks subsets of fast-acting interneurons contributing to the higher-order brain centers mushroom bodies and central complex. Taken together, our work expands the known functional range of foxQ2 genes from sensory and neurosecretory cell specification to interneurons involved in the function of higher-order brain centers.

articles.title: CREBBP variants underlying Menke-Hennekam syndrome exhibit histone acetyltransferase hyperactivity with divergent phase behaviors
articles.abstract: Menke–Hennekam syndrome (MKHK) is a neurodevelopmental disease characterized by specific pathogenic regions within the transcriptional coactivator CREB–binding protein (CREBBP) . CREBBP regulates gene expression through histone acetyltransferase (HAT) activity and involves IDR–dependent transcriptional condensates. Although domain-specific phenotypes and distinct DNA methylation episignatures have been recognized in MKHK, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain widely unclear. In this study, we identified a recurrent missense variant, p.(R1868W) [R1868W]) and a novel splice variant r.5963_5969del,p.(Cys1723Thrfs*19) [C1723fs] in two families clinically diagnosed with MKHK and manifesting developmental delay, characteristic facial features, and growth impairment. R1868W and C1723fs exhibited increased auto–, nonhistone protein, and histone acetylation. Despite these shared enzymatic abnormalities, the variants promoted divergent disruption in liquid–liquid phase separation.
