Earthworm vibrations were detected best at 200 Hz and were detected significantly more in wetter than in drier soils. Moreover, in wetter soils, vibrations induced by detritivores were detected more frequently and at higher intensities than those of geophages. These findings suggest differences in activity levels between detritivores and geophages, as a function of soil moisture content. The observed activity patterns are likely to have food web consequences because earthworm consumers relying on mechanoreceptors to detect prey might detect detritivores more often, specifically in wetter soils.

articles.title: Synthesis, spectroscopic study, antioxidant, DNA-cleavage and enzyme-mimicking activities for metal(II/III) complexes with azo ligand–eugenol scaffold
articles.abstract: A newly synthesized azo ligand, 1-((5-allyl-2-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl)diazenyl)anthracene-9,10-dione (H-MND), derived from an anthraquinone nucleus coupled with the natural phenol (eugenol), was employed to prepare Co(II), Ni(II), Cu(II), Rh(III) and Pd(II) complexes, with the ligand proposed to adopt a tridentate coordination mode. Anthraquinone derivatives and natural phenols are recognized for diverse pharmacological activities, making them valuable scaffolds for the design of bioactive ligands. The synthesized compounds were characterized by FT-IR, UV–vis, NMR spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, elemental analysis, thermal analysis thermogravimetric-differential scanning calorimetry (TGA-DSC), assessment of chlorine content, magnetic susceptibility and molar conductance measurements, which collectively suggested predominantly non-electrolytic behaviour. In the 1,1-diphenyl-2-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) assay, the Ni(II) complex exhibited the highest antioxidant activity among the synthesized compounds, with an IC50 value significantly different from that of gallic acid (t = 4.31, p ˂ 0.01). Only the Pd(II) complex displayed activity towards plasmid DNA consistent with partial cleavage in the absence of externally added redox agents. Furthermore, activity mimicking phenoxazinone synthase was evaluated for the Cu(II) and Co(II) complexes, revealing system-specific catalytic behaviour. These results support further investigation into the biomedical and catalytic potential of these metal complexes.

articles.title: The paradox of neutral carbonate budgets on coral-dominated reefs
articles.abstract: Coral reefs deliver vital services via a complex three-dimensional framework sustained by the balance between calcium carbonate production and erosion, or the net carbonate budget state. In many tropical western Atlantic reefs, ecological decline has reduced carbonate production, yielding near-neutral or negative budgets. Yet some reefs retain high coral cover and, theoretically, should also have high net positive budgets, yet often show modest carbonate accumulation. We used the remote reef of Cayo Arenas in the Campeche Bank, Gulf of Mexico, to test whether in reefs under suboptimal (variable) environmental conditions, high coral production is offset by robust bioeroder communities, producing neutral budgets. At 14 sites, we quantified carbonate producers and bioeroders to estimate gross production, bioerosion and net budget states. Despite relatively high live coral cover, mean net carbonate budgets did not differ significantly from a neutral (zero) state, despite a positive net budget (0.7 ± 0.5 SE kg CaCO3 m−2 yr−1) and substantial site-to-site variability (range: −2.3 to 4.3 kg CaCO3 m−2 yr−1). Crucially, this neutrality arose not from depressed biological activity (as in degraded reefs) but from an active equilibrium: elevated carbonate production coupled with substantial bioerosion. These reefs, therefore, represent a contemporary, functional reef state in net stasis. Distinguishing active-neutral reefs, where both production and bioerosion are elevated, from impoverishment-neutral reefs, where both are suppressed, is critical for predicting reef trajectories under environmental change and for targeting management, although near-stasis emerging from high carbonate turnover can appear functionally intact yet operate with limited buffering capacity against net carbonate loss.

articles.title: Variation in cultural attitude, knowledge and individual motivational factors impact engagement and tool use in a field experiment in wild chimpanzees
articles.abstract: Cultural traditions shape how animals approach ecological problems. Over the last two decades, Ugandan chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) have engaged with the honey-trap experiment, an apparatus mimicking a beehive, while relying on their cultural knowledge. Here, we compared the behaviour of three Ugandan chimpanzee communities in the experiment, adding a previously untested community, the Mwera South chimpanzees of Bugoma Forest. First, we tested whether communities varied in their engagement with the experiment and investigated whether differences lay in individual or community-based characteristics. Second, we analysed individual variation within the same culture, particularly focusing on the new data coming from Bugoma Forest. We found that only the Kanyawara chimpanzees of Kibale Forest displayed a dedicated instrumental method, stick use, realized in their cultural knowledge and expressed by most members of the community, congruent with the largest engagement with the resource and suggestive of a general positive cultural attitude towards honey. By contrast, the two other communities appeared to lack a cultural attitude towards honey, with no attached tool technique overall. Nevertheless, there were also large inter-individual differences. Notably, Bugoma chimpanzees displayed undescribed behavioural flexibility, using a range of tool behaviours, including both stick and leaf tool use, a pattern never documented before. Cultural attitudes toward resources thus constitute an additional layer to culture in addition to instrumental knowledge and coexist with individual motivational traits in influencing the realization of cultural behaviour.

articles.title: When feathers fell from fashion: unpacking the end of the UK plumage trade
articles.abstract: By the mid-twentieth century, the previously booming bird feather trade was a fraction of what it was in its prime, allowing for the recovery of many bird species. We use a qualitative impact evaluation method to assign probable causality to different drivers of this change, ultimately providing expert-supported explanations of how a large-scale behaviour change was enacted to benefit conservation. We outline a method for applying general elimination methodology plus (GEM+), accounting for different facets of evidence reliability, to generate conclusions on most strongly supported causes of change. GEM+ addresses calls for an increase in impact evaluation in conservation, which will require a range of tools, including qualitative, to fill. Analysis of diverse evidence using GEM+ suggests that conservation advocacy, interacting with broader contextual factors, plausibly contributed to a shift in public behaviour that was instrumental in the passage of the Plumage Act and the subsequent end of the trade. This case study has widespread implications for designing effective behaviour change campaigns, as well as providing a framework for conducting impact evaluations in a range of conservation settings.

articles.title: A continuous confinement-deconfinement transition in a triangular quantum magnet
articles.abstract: A continuous transition between phases hosting distinct excitations—bosonic magnons versus fermionic spinons—is a long-sought phenomenon in quantum magnetism, analogous to the confinement-deconfinement transition in quantum chromodynamics. We report evidence for such a transition in the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet thallium ytterbium disulfide. Antiferromagnetic order develops below T N ≈ 0.53 kelvin. A c -axis field suppresses this order, driving the system into a gapless quantum spin liquid with a spinon Fermi surface above μ 0 H c ≈ 3 T , evidenced by a finite residual linear term in thermal conductivity, a Pauli-like susceptibility, and a temperature-independent nuclear magnetic resonance Knight shift. Approaching H c from above, the scattering rate of itinerant excitations is strongly enhanced, while their density of states shows no critical enhancement, atypical of conventional magnetic quantum criticality. These results point to a continuous confinement-deconfinement transition governed by fractionalized excitations beyond the Ginzburg-Landau paradigm.

articles.title: A phosphorylation-gated GAPDH-MAPK6-LBD1 module controls drought-responsive transcription
articles.abstract: Drought adaptation requires rapid spatial reorganization of signaling proteins to reprogram stress-responsive transcription, yet how phosphorylation coordinates this process remains unclear. Here we aimed to define how phosphorylation-gated protein relocalization regulates a BpLBD1-centered drought pathway in Betula platyphylla (birch). Drought activated two kinase branches: BpAGC phosphorylated BpMAPK6 at Ser318 within a cryptic nuclear localization signal, promoting importin α recognition, whereas BpCKII phosphorylated BpGAPDH at Thr109, Thr270, Ser279 and Thr298, promoting importin β recognition. Dual phosphorylation enabled coordinated nuclear accumulation of BpMAPK6 and BpGAPDH. In the nucleus, phosphorylated BpGAPDH acted as a scaffold-like adaptor coupling BpMAPK6 to BpLBD1, enabling BpMAPK6-mediated phosphorylation of BpLBD1 at Ser29. This weakened BpLBD1 binding to the BpMYB123 promoter, reduced expression of the drought-sensitivity regulator BpMYB123 , and de-repressed drought-responsive genes such as BpRD29B . Disrupting BpGAPDH or BpLBD1 Ser29 phosphorylation compromised drought tolerance. Thus, a phospho-spatial GAPDH-MAPK6-LBD1 switch couples nuclear protein assembly to drought-responsive transcription.

articles.title: Accessing invasion-competent Plasmodium vivax merozoites reveals antibody-dependent NK cell activation
articles.abstract: Malaria pathogenesis and clinical symptoms arise from blood-stage replication of Plasmodium parasites, which depends on rapid invasion of red blood cells by merozoites. Despite the central importance of this stage, direct functional studies of Plasmodium vivax ( P. vivax ) merozoites remain limited by the lack of continuous in vitro culture and restricted access to viable, invasion-competent merozoites from clinical isolates. Consequently, key aspects of P. vivax merozoite biology and immune recognition remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a robust platform enabling synchronized release and high-yield isolation of invasion-competent P. vivax merozoites from ex vivo cultures. Reversible inhibition of parasite egress using the PKG inhibitor ML10 enables synchronization at the segmented schizont stage, followed by rapid mechanical release of merozoites using a liposome-based extrusion approach. This workflow yields highly pure merozoites with recovery rates exceeding 75% while preserving structural integrity and invasive capacity. Leveraging this platform, we demonstrate that antibody-opsonized P. vivax merozoites activate human natural killer cells, revealing functional antibody-dependent immune responses.

articles.title: All-soft organic electrochemical diodes based on asymmetric active layers for signal isolation in deformable electronics
articles.abstract: All-soft electronics have emerged as a promising platform for deformable and human-centric systems, yet the development of mechanically compliant diodes remains a major challenge due to limitations in material compatibility, device architecture, and stable operation under deformation. Electrochemical approaches offer a viable route to address this challenge by enabling bulk, low-voltage charge modulation in soft materials without relying on rigid junction interfaces. Here, we report, to the best of our knowledge, the first all-soft organic electrochemical diode (OECD) based on an asymmetric active-layer geometry. The device incorporates a transfer-printed ultrathin ion-gel interface that preserves conformal coverage and the active electrochemical architecture under strain. The device achieves high rectification through polarity-dependent electrochemical potential redistribution, with a rectification ratio of up to 2.23 × 10 4 at ±1 V and stable operation under tensile strains of up to 30% and repeated mechanical deformation. This ion-gel-based architecture preserves the electrochemical asymmetry required for diode operation while maintaining structural integrity under strain. Beyond the individual device, the all-soft OECD enables deformable rectifiers and logic gates and functions as a key signal-isolation element that suppresses cross-talk in a deformable pressure-sensing array. These results establish an electrochemical diode platform that combines mechanical deformability, high rectification performance, and circuit-level compatibility, providing a pathway toward fully deformable and integrated human-centric electronic systems.

articles.title: Anomalous phonon selection rules and Raman optical activity in RuO2
articles.abstract: Breakdown of selection rules and emergence of optical activity in Raman spectroscopy typically signal symmetry-breaking events essential for understanding novel phases of solids. Here, we apply our recently developed rotational anisotropy Raman spectroscopy technique to single-crystal ruthenium dioxide—a compound of recent interest as a candidate workhorse material for altermagnetism yet whose magnetic ground state remains under intense debate. Our data reveal a salient breakdown of selection rules for zone-center phonons, accompanied by clear splitting in the angle-dependent polarimetry plots for the two opposite helicity-nonconserving circularly polarized scattering channels. These observations provide definitive evidence of a previously overlooked symmetry-breaking event, involving either spatial or time-reversal symmetry. In either scenario, the underlying mechanism is likely a bulk hidden order parameter, potentially involving multipole moments of Ruthenium(IV) set by the local crystal field environment. Our work demonstrates how subtle symmetry-breaking events can manifest through lattice dynamics and calls for renewed experimental and theoretical efforts to map the phase diagram of ruthenium dioxide as a system poised near quantum phase transition boundaries.

articles.title: BCG vaccination mitigates tau pathology and restores cognitive function in PS19 mice
articles.abstract: Retrospective studies in patients with nonmuscle invasive bladder cancer have reported a significant reduction in Alzheimer’s disease incidence (12 to 78%) among Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) recipients versus controls. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, we evaluated BCG in the PS19 mouse model of tauopathy. We found that BCG administration reduced hippocampal phospho-tau and microgliosis while preserving neuronal markers. In vivo volumetric T2–magnetic resonance Imaging (MRI) demonstrated attenuation of brain atrophy accompanied by increased glutamate-weighted chemical exchange saturation transfer–MRI signals. Functionally, BCG-treated mice showed improved performance in the novel object recognition test, as well as improved body-weight maintenance and survival. Transcriptomic profiling of the hippocampus revealed near complete normalization of the PS19 disease-associated gene expression signature toward that of healthy controls. Flow cytometric profiling of brain myeloid populations demonstrated a reduction in activated resident microglia, but total microglia cells remain elevated. Moreover, an increase of trained immunity marker CD80 on the recruited peripheral myeloid cells ensues following BCG treatment. Consistent with this shift in myeloid state, primary brain myeloid cells from BCG-treated mice also exhibited enhanced phagocytosis of fluorescein isothiocyanate-labeled tau fibrils and increased lactate production. Together, these findings indicate that BCG induces systemic and central nervous system myeloid cell reprogramming that limits neuroinflammation, enhances tau clearance, and rescues cognitive and neurodegenerative phenotypes in a tauopathy model. BCG is a safe, readily available therapy that merits consideration as a preventive agent against dementia.

articles.title: Building digital pregnancies from the single cell up
articles.abstract: Single-cell digital twins connect in vitro drug screening studies with clinical outcomes, providing a new framework to evaluate therapies and advance precision medicine in pregnancy.

articles.title: CCAN forms the spherical shell-like structure in interphase kinetochores
articles.abstract: The kinetochore is an essential structure for the faithful chromosome segregation during mitosis. The 16-protein complex known as the constitutive centromere-associated network (CCAN) localizes the centromere throughout the cell cycle and forms the basis of the kinetochore. Although cryo–electron microscopy has provided a structural model of an individual CCAN unit, how multiple CCAN units are organized within cells remains unclear. Here, using in silico and in vivo analyses, we demonstrate that multiple CCAN units form a spherical shell-like structure in interphase DT40 kinetochores. CENP-T and CENP-N localize to the CCAN shell, whereas the CENP-C cupin domain clusters at the center. Molecular dynamics simulations of CCAN assembly suggest that CENP-C–DNA interactions constrain the orientation of CCAN units, supporting a spherical shell-like organization via CENP-C oligomerization. Super-resolution imaging reveals the spherical shell-like structure at DT40 kinetochores, and CENP-C knockout or expression of a CENP-C DNA binding deficient mutant abolishes the structure, consistent with the simulation-derived model. These findings provide important insights into the spatial organization of functional kinetochores within cells.

articles.title: CREBBP loss drives immune evasion by epigenetically silencing STING and MHC-I in small cell lung cancer
articles.abstract: Most small cell lung cancers (SCLCs) exhibit low immunogenicity and intrinsic resistance to immunotherapy, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identify CREBBP loss, a frequent genetic alteration in SCLC, as a key suppressor of tumor cell-intrinsic immune responses that drives an immune-cold tumor microenvironment in Rb1/Trp53 -driven autochthonous mouse models. Consistently, Crebbp deletion promotes immune escape in syngeneic SCLC models. Mechanistically, Crebbp loss suppresses Sting and major histocompatibility complex class-I expression by reducing histone H3 acetylation. Notably, HDAC inhibition restores histone acetylation, reactivates these silenced genes, and induces tumor cell-intrinsic immune responses. Moreover, pharmacological HDAC inhibition synergizes with immune checkpoint blockade to suppress tumor growth in both Crebbp -mutant and Crebbp -wild-type SCLCs, with a more prominent effect in Crebbp -mutant tumors. Collectively, these findings establish CREBBP loss as a key mechanism of immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance in SCLC, highlighting HDAC inhibition as a promising strategy to enhance immunotherapy efficacy.

articles.title: Hearing the shape of an arena with spectral swarm robotics
articles.abstract: Swarm robotics relies on robots with minimal sensing and computation that achieve self-organization at the level of the collective to address a variety of tasks. Yet, swarm robotics still struggles with global tasks that require understanding the broader spatial context in which robots operate, such as identifying the shape of the arena in which they are embedded. Here, we introduce spectral swarm robotics, a framework in which robots recover global spectral descriptors of the swarm’s geometric structure through strictly local interactions. To do so, robots emulate diffusion to locally estimate Laplacian spectral invariants, quantities normally obtained only through centralized computation. These spectral values serve as compact descriptors of the environment. In the present proof of concept, robots estimated the second Laplacian eigenvalue, λ 2 , and used it to classify arenas from a predefined set of shapes with distinct spectral signatures. We show that estimating a single eigenvalue is sufficient for one-shot classification among selected confined environments with distinct spectral signatures. We uncovered a scaling law linking swarm size (a global parameter) and interaction radius (a local parameter) that ensures robust estimation. We validated the approach experimentally on two distinct hardware platforms, Kilobots and Pogobots, achieving reliable classification of arena shapes under realistic noise and sparse connectivity conditions. Last, we discuss how locally recovering Laplacian spectral invariants opens avenues for swarm robotics in settings where producing efficient collective behaviors strongly depends on the global structure of the swarm.

articles.title: Reducing energy and air consumption in scuba diving with underwater exoskeletons
articles.abstract: Assisting underwater locomotion with exoskeletons could reduce energy and air consumption during scuba diving.

articles.title: Structural bias enables reliable sim-to-real transfer in reinforcement learning for robot swarms
articles.abstract: Reinforcement learning offers a powerful framework for automatically generating control policies for robot swarms, yet its application to physical multirobot systems has been limited by the simulation-to-reality gap. Despite substantial advances in multiagent reinforcement learning, systematic demonstrations of gradient-based sim-to-real transfer to physical robot swarms remain scarce. Most work remains confined to simulation, and the few real-robot demonstrations lack evaluation across multiple runs and tasks. We show that this barrier can be overcome by embedding structural constraints into policy learning. We introduce attention-based counterfactual policy gradients for behavior selection in robot swarms (SwarmACB), a multiagent actor-critic method in which robots arbitrate among predefined behavior modules—reactive sensorimotor routines such as phototaxis or aggregation—rather than learning low-level motor commands. This architectural choice reduces the variance of learned solutions, which we argue mitigates overfitting to simulation artifacts. Through systematic evaluation on five collective missions using 20 physical e-puck robots (250 real-robot runs), we demonstrate that SwarmACB transfers successfully from simulation to reality, substantially outperforming continuous-action baselines. By progressively constraining policy architecture, perception, and model capacity, we show that smaller, structured policies transfer more reliably than large, unconstrained ones. These findings challenge the assumption that scale is necessary for successful transfer, suggesting instead that principled structural design enables reinforcement learning to produce control software for robot swarms that is both learned automatically and directly deployable in the physical world.

articles.title: A 5 + 1 polyene scaffold that selectively recognizes ergosterol’s conjugated diene uncouples antifungal potency from host toxicity
articles.abstract: Amphotericin B remains the gold-standard therapy for invasive fungal infections, but its clinical utility is limited by toxicity arising from poor selectivity for fungal ergosterol over mammalian cholesterol, a challenge that decades of medicinal chemistry have failed to fully overcome. Here, we report mandimycin M16, a polyene macrolide engineered from a unique 5 + 1 polyene scaffold that uncouples antifungal potency from host toxicity. Mandimycin M16 exhibited potent, broad-spectrum activity against 11 tested World Health Organization (WHO) priority fungal pathogens. Unlike amphotericin B, which binds cholesterol, M16 exhibited no detectable cholesterol binding and showed no detectable hemolysis, cytotoxicity, or nephrotoxicity at concentrations up to 128 micrograms per milliliter in vitro and after up to seven daily intravenous doses in mice. Mechanistic studies revealed that mandimycin M16 exerted rapid fungicidal activity through selective recognition of the conjugated C5–C8 diene system present in ergosterol but absent in cholesterol, a mode of sterol discrimination fundamentally different from classical polyenes. In multiple disseminated murine infection models, M16 outperformed liposomal amphotericin B at equivalent doses, achieving up to 3.4 log reduction in fungal burden and 100% survival without detectable renal injury by biomarkers or histopathology. These findings establish that the 5 + 1 polyene architecture enables complete sterol selectivity and molecularly uncouples antifungal potency from host toxicity, providing a next-generation antifungal candidate for the treatment of invasive fungal infections.

articles.title: A fluorescent choline kinase alpha inhibitor for intraoperative molecular imaging during resection of canine NSCLC tumors
articles.abstract: Choline kinase α (ChoKα) is a biomarker of lung cancer, is overexpressed in 60% of human pulmonary malignancies, and is associated with an aggressive phenotype and poor clinical outcome. Patients with lung cancer who undergo surgery have a recurrence rate of 30 to 50%, indicating a potential need for better tumor detection modalities. A near-infrared fluorescent ChoKα-targeting imaging agent, JAS239 (λ ex , λ em : 745, 775 nanometers), was developed for intraoperative identification of tumors, their margins, and local metastases. In lung cancer cells, JAS239 inhibited phosphocholine production, reduced viability in a dose-dependent manner, and accumulated in the cytoplasm where ChoKα is active. JAS239 had favorable pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics for imaging metastatic lung lesions in mice. In situ and ex vivo fluorescence imaging of primary lung tumors in a canine clinical trial showed distinct tumor identification and margin delineation with a tumor-to-background ratio of 5.0 ± 0.6 and a contrast-to-variance ratio of 2.0 ± 0.2 at 0.5 milligram/kilogram. Fluorescence imaging identified a clinically significant event where an occult lesion was found after primary tumor resection. Fluorescence imaging also identified a close surgical margin, which prompted further investigation. Immunohistochemistry for ChoKα showed overexpression in canine lung tumors proportional to tumor fluorescence. Ex vivo human tumor painting demonstrated preferential JAS239 localization with a tumor-to-background ratio of 1.5 ± 0.1 and a contrast-to-variance ratio of 0.9 ± 0.1. These studies establish JAS239 as a safe and effective imaging agent for intraoperative lung tumor detection, warranting further evaluation for human patients with lung cancer.

articles.title: Cas9 nickase–mediated contraction of CAG/CTG repeats is associated with phenotypic improvements in a Huntington’s disease mouse model
articles.abstract: Expanded CAG/CTG repeats cause more than 15 different diseases that all remain without a disease-modifying treatment. Because repeat length accounts for most of the variation in disease severity, contracting CAG/CTG repeats presents an attractive therapeutic avenue. Here, we show that the CRISPR-Cas9 nickase targeted to CAG/CTG repeats leads to efficient repeat contractions in Huntington’s disease (HD) patient–derived neurons and astrocytes and in myotonic dystrophy type 1 patient–derived neurons. The approach was allele selective and free of detectable off-target mutations. Injection of the Cas9 nickase into the striatum of the R6/1 mouse model of HD using adeno-associated viral vectors led to repeat contractions in more than half of striatal neurons. Upon injection, we observed a reduction in the number of inclusion bodies, an improved gene expression profile, and amelioration of locomotion deficits in the open field test. The effects were greater than expected from the contractions induced, suggesting that non–cell autonomous mechanisms may be involved. Our results provide the proof of concept that correction of CAG/CTG repeats can improve HD phenotypes in a mouse disease model.

articles.title: Erratum for the Research Article “Systematic analysis of cellular cross-talk reveals a role for SEMA6D-TREM2 regulating microglial function in Alzheimer’s disease”
Graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis shapes T cell biology and immune reconstitution after hematopoietic cell transplant
articles.abstract: Successful hematopoietic cell transplant requires immunosuppression to prevent graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), a lethal, T cell–mediated complication. The phase 3 BMT CTN 1703 trial demonstrated superior GVHD-free/relapse-free survival for posttransplant cyclophosphamide (PT-Cy)–based GVHD prophylaxis versus tacrolimus/methotrexate (Tac/MTX), but the T cell biology underpinning these outcomes remains unknown. To determine this, 324 patients were coenrolled onto BMT CTN 1801 to investigate the distinct T cell immune reconstitution pathways of these regimens, including extensive evaluation of T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire, via sequencing of 2359 longitudinal samples and 180,432,350 T cells. Multimodal T cell analysis revealed that PT-Cy was associated with pan–T cell deletion followed by delayed T cell expansion from a smaller founder population compared with Tac/MTX. This created a T cell diversity bottleneck, leading to reduced TCR repertoire diversity for 2 years posttransplant. Reduced TCR diversity, more common in patients receiving PT-Cy, was linked to protection against chronic GVHD when patients were analyzed without regard to study arm. Leveraging donor- and host-specific TCR clonal analysis, we determined that PT-Cy–mediated T cell depletion also depleted pathogen-specific TCRs, rendering PT-Cy patients more likely to lack detectable graft-derived pathogen-specific TCRs early after transplant, which was associated with an increased risk of severe infection. This study reveals how distinct immunosuppression strategies uniquely remodel T cell immunity and shape divergent transplant outcomes.

articles.title: Single-nucleotide polymorphism–directed design of allele-specific antisense oligonucleotides for spinocerebellar ataxia type 3
articles.abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), also called Machado-Joseph disease, the most common form of autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia, is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in ATXN3 . The mutant protein is prone to aggregation and exerts toxic gain-of-function effects, whereas the wild-type protein has important neuroprotective roles as a deubiquitinase. Current treatment strategies for SCA3 lack specificity for the mutant allele. Identifying genetic variants such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in linkage with the pathogenic CAG expansion offers a promising avenue to develop allele-specific therapeutic interventions, like antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs). To address this, we conducted allele-specific, targeted, multiplexed nanopore sequencing on 79 patients with SCA3 from Germany, UK, and Portugal. We identified almost 200 polymorphisms and grouped them into three haplotype blocks on the basis of linkage disequilibrium. These SNPs were strongly associated with the CAG expansion. Genotypic modeling of our subcohorts indicated that targeting only two SNPs from different blocks could enable allele-specific treatment of the majority of European patients with SCA3. We evaluated 17 candidate ASOs targeting SNPs from different haplotype blocks. Seven of these ASOs caused allele-preferential reduction of more than 65%. A single ASO application in two SCA3 iPSC-derived cortical neurons (AX1, AX2) achieved up to 90% reduction of mutant ATXN3. Toxicity assessments together with RNA sequencing analyses in AX1 did not indicate evidence of toxicity or widespread transcriptional perturbations. These findings highlight that characterizing heterozygosity rates offers valuable opportunities for selective ASO therapies. Our proof-of-principle targeting with ASOs demonstrates the feasibility of haplotype-informed allele-specific silencing in ATXN3 .

articles.title: Targeting ZIP12-mediated Zn2+ signaling as a treatment for pulmonary hypertension
articles.abstract: ZIP12, a membrane-bound zinc importer, is up-regulated in the remodeled pulmonary arterioles of patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Genetic deletion of its encoding gene, Slc39a12 , ameliorates the disease in rodent models. Here, we show that ZIP12 overexpression in human pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMCs) increased intracellular labile Zn 2+ and promoted proliferation. ZIP12 siRNA knockdown attenuated pulmonary hypertension in rodent models. We developed a humanized anti-ZIP12 monoclonal antibody, APL-9796, that normalized intracellular Zn 2+ concentration, suppressed proliferation in fibroblasts derived from patients with PAH and PDGF-stimulated PASMCs, and reduced PDGF-induced cytoskeletal remodeling in PASMCs and contractility in PASMCs and engineered pulmonary artery tissues. APL-9796 showed dose-dependent efficacy in humanized Slc39a12 rats, improving cardiopulmonary parameters after induction of pulmonary hypertension and was well tolerated in phase 1 clinical studies. Transcriptomic profiling revealed modulation of several molecular pathways, including those involving AMPK, PPAR, and PI3K-Akt. ZIP12-driven labile Zn 2+ signaling underpins the pathogenesis of PAH. Targeting ZIP12 with APL-9796 offers a promising therapeutic strategy.

articles.title: The kinase inhibitor dabrafenib halts progression of cerebral cavernous malformations in a BRAF-independent manner
articles.abstract: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) constitute the second most common type of intracranial vascular malformations. Cavernomas arise because of somatic or autosomal dominant inherited loss-of-function mutations in CCM genes, forming fragile mulberry-like malformed blood vessel structures that are prone to leak and break. Treatment is limited to surgical removal of solitary cavernomas, and because patients often present with multiple lesions, pharmacological alternatives to surgery are needed. We performed a high-throughput screen of 5200 bioactive molecules in programmed cell death 10 (PDCD10 or CCM3)–deficient mouse endothelial cells, coupled to automated image analysis. This screen identified dabrafenib, a clinically approved BRAF inhibitor, as a compound that restored cell-cell junctions and vascular barrier properties of CCM3-deficient endothelial cells. The potential translatability of dabrafenib was tested in acute and chronic CCM mouse models, where it reduced cerebral lesion burden and suppressed lesion permeability. Dabrafenib also rescued abnormal structural defects present in the developing retina vasculature in an acute CCM mouse model. Mechanistically, dabrafenib targeted extracellular regulated kinase (ERK)5–Krüppel-like factor (KLF)2/4 signaling and suppressed F-actin stress fiber formation in human brain endothelial cells, two potentially independent and central molecular processes involved in CCM pathology. Silencing BRAF did not prevent dabrafenib-induced KLF2/4 inhibition or restoration of cell-cell junctions, suggesting that its dual therapeutic outcome is independent of BRAF pathway inhibition. In conclusion, dabrafenib is a low–molecular weight compound that inhibits cavernoma pathogenesis, suggesting that CCMs could be treated with dabrafenib to block cavernoma growth and vascular leakage.

articles.title: Brazilian butt lifts and vampire facials in England are targeted in government crackdown
articles.abstract: New restrictions on “high risk” cosmetic surgical procedures in England have been announced by ministers as they vowed to crack down on “cowboys” putting patients at risk.1The new rules aim to ensure that cosmetic procedures such as liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), so called vampire facials, and chemical peels can be carried out only by certain healthcare professionals.Cosmetic surgery and other high risk procedures, such as those listed above, will also be banned for under-18s, the government announced. But procedures provided by the NHS for treating a medical condition such as rhinoplasty, otoplasty, or breast reduction could still be available on a case-by-case basis. Facial botox and lip fillers are already banned for children.2Rogue providers found breaking the rules will face new criminal offences and risk unlimited fines or fixed penalties up to £4000.The Department of Health and Social Care said that the new rules would “close a dangerous loophole”...

articles.title: Conflict and climate change are driving food shortages
articles.abstract: The world is still producing more calories per capita year on year, despite a growing population.12 Yet localised food shortages continue to occur across the globe, driven primarily by conflict,34 and also increasingly by climate change.5Conflict affects all dimensions of food security:67 production is affected as land is either abandoned or harder to cultivate and people are displaced; access to markets is restricted; and people are less able to afford sufficient food.4 There are long term negative impacts on health, manifested particularly in the increased prevalence of stunting.8The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and World Food Programme 2026 Global Report on Food Crises identifies 13 countries and territories where acute food insecurity is expected to increase.9 Twelve of these 13 hotspots are affected by armed conflict and violence, and risk of famine is identified in four: Sudan, South Sudan, Gaza Strip, and Somalia.10 More broadly, around 60%-70% of the world’s...

articles.title: Green transition provides a crucial opportunity to finance universal health coverage
articles.abstract: The green energy transition is opening up potential sources of new finance that could be used to fund universal health coverage (UHC) in low and middle income countries. Fossil fuel subsidies—government support that keeps energy prices below supply costs, whether through direct payments, state owned utility losses, or price controls—can account for a large proportion of government spending.1 Reducing these subsidies as part of a shift away from fossil fuels, alongside introducing carbon pricing and capturing new royalties from critical minerals, would provide extra resources for public services. Health systems, which bear current and future health consequences of fossil fuel use and mining activities, have a strong argument for benefiting from these resources, but how much reaches those in greatest need will depend on political decisions and good governance.Fossil fuel subsidies crowd out health spendingFossil fuel subsidies remain large, widespread, and acutely sensitive to international oil prices. When Russia invaded...

articles.title: Living with POTS during weather changes
articles.abstract: I have lived with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) for over 12 years. It affects me every day and no single day is ever the same. Several things can trigger a flare, including changes in temperature and atmospheric pressure. The recent summer heatwaves were very challenging. I had to postpone going to hospital for scheduled treatment as I knew that the lack of ventilation or air conditioning there would make me feel unwell, and this would have a knock-on effect on my treatment response.Extreme weatherBecause of POTS, my body struggles to regulate its temperature, and this makes me prone to heat stroke. I experience sun sensitivity and altered sweating capacity, and changes in air temperature can make me light headed and dizzy. As a result, I tend to not socialise or stay out when it is very warm during the day, which can be isolating.I have found several ways to...

articles.title: Measuring the impact of conflict on the climate
articles.abstract: Greenhouse gases resulting from armed conflicts are a serious problem. Recent wars in Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran have highlighted the immense potential costs of armed conflict to the climate and overall ecological health of people and Earth. The first 14 days of the Iran war alone produced more than the total climate pollution of Iceland in 2024—roughly five million tonnes of carbon dioxide.1 Five years of war in Ukraine has released almost 311 million tonnes of carbon dioxide—the equivalent of annual emissions in France.2 In Gaza, carbon emissions during the first 15 months of the conflict were more than 30 million tonnes—equivalent to the amount of carbon absorbed by 33 million acres of forests in a year.3Although these estimates provide a window into the climate damage of war, still no international climate agreement requirements exist for governments to report these emissions. Citing national security concerns, the US Congress lobbied and...

articles.title: Medical news in brief: Weekly insulin ȷab approved, doctors “bullied and harassed” at work, UK bans weight loss pill ads, and other stories
articles.abstract: Type 2 diabetesWeekly insulin jab is approved by MHRAThe UK Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency approved the weekly insulin injection efsitora alfa, also known as Onswik and made by Eli Lilly, for adults with type 2 diabetes. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommended the treatment in August, citing clinical trial evidence showing that the drug was as effective as long acting insulins already widely used to treat type 2 diabetes. Unlike current options, Onswik needs to be injected only once a week.Staff wellbeingNHS England staff are reluctant to raise concernsNHS England is a “challenging” environment to work in and staff are unwilling to raise concerns, a report found. The internal Freedom to Speak Up (FTSU) report said that staff who raised concerns faced bullying, harassment, and psychological abuse from seniors.1 In 2025-26 NHS England staff raised 235 FTSU cases, after 319 cases in 2024-25. Issues included...

articles.title: War and military mobilisation are drivers of climate change
articles.abstract: Hard edged national security leaders talk about climate change as a “threat multiplier.”1 By this they mean climate change may cause instability and potentially provoke armed conflict as regions become dangerously hot, wet, or dry, and as societies and governments are stressed beyond their capacity to cope.23The US military, the UK Ministry of Defence, NATO, and the UN Security Council have all used the climate change as a threat multiplier frame.45 Following this logic many governments have now added climate change related threats to their rationales for increased defence spending and military capability.6Framing and acting as if climate change is a threat multiplier ignores how war is a climate change multiplier. The greenhouse gas emissions from war and preparations for it make climate change worse. And adding climate change to the military’s portfolio may be unnecessary and counterproductive.The consequences of climate change are becoming as deadly as war—in some regions,...

articles.title: Water rarely starts wars, but wars increasingly damage water systems
articles.abstract: In 1995 Ismail Serageldin of the World Bank predicted that “the wars of the next century will be fought over water.”1 Three decades on, the forecast has not quite come true. Serageldin himself now locates the risk within states, more so than between them.2 Water scarcity seldom starts wars, but it can compound grievances that weak institutions leave unresolved. War, in turn, degrades the water systems on which health and recovery depend, entrenching the fragility that reproduces violence. This is a mutually reinforcing cycle. Without water there is neither health nor durable peace. Without peace, water is never secure.Water compounds conflict but is seldom the only causeSyria’s 2007-2009 drought is often invoked as the trigger of the 2011 uprising. Satellite, meteorological, and field data tell a different story. Agriculture rebounded strongly in 2010, and pre-war migration was largely internal, temporary, and adaptive.3 Vulnerability had accumulated over decades of water-intensive, subsidised...

articles.title: [Articles] Disease-free survival and overall survival after neoadjuvant immunotherapy in mismatch repair-deficient colon cancer in the Netherlands: results of the single-arm, multicentre, phase 2, NICHE-2 trial
articles.abstract: In patients with locally advanced dMMR colon cancer, treatment with ipilimumab and nivolumab before surgery resulted in a 3-year disease-free survival and 5-year overall survival of 100%. These findings support neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab as a potential standard of care for patients with locally advanced dMMR colon cancer.

articles.title: [Articles] Endometrial ablation plus levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system versus endometrial ablation alone in women with heavy menstrual bleeding in The Netherlands (MIRA2): a multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled, superiority trial
articles.abstract: The combination of endometrial ablation and LNG-IUS significantly reduced the incidence of hysterectomy compared with endometrial ablation alone. The combined treatment appears to be a safe adjunctive strategy for heavy menstrual bleeding that does not increase the risk of complications.

articles.title: [Comment] Preserving the uterus: an effective dual therapy to avoid hysterectomy
articles.abstract: Heavy menstrual bleeding is a challenging condition that, when refractory to conventional treatment, frequently culminates in hysterectomy. Endometrial ablation offers an effective, uterus-sparing alternative for women who do not desire future childbearing, with lower perioperative morbidity and faster recovery than hysterectomy.1–3 However, the durability of this procedure can be variable. Residual endometrium can result in recurrent bleeding or cyclical pelvic pain requiring further treatment, with approximately one in ten women undergoing hysterectomy within 2 years.

articles.title: [Comment] Redefining curative treatment for early-stage mismatch repair-deficient colon cancer
articles.abstract: For decades, the standard of care for patients with resected stage II and III colon cancer has centred on surgery with consideration of postoperative adjuvant systemic therapy to reduce risk of recurrence. Mismatch repair deficiency is seen in 10–15% of non-metastatic colon cancers and is predictive of response to immune checkpoint inhibition. The initial report of the single-arm, phase 2 NICHE-2 study of one dose of ipilimumab (1 mg per kg) and two doses of nivolumab (3 mg per kg) before surgery with clinical stage II and III colon cancer generated considerable interest after demonstrating a remarkable 98% pathologic response rate, including a pathologic complete response rate of 68%.

articles.title: Advancing functional treatment prediction for precision oncology
articles.abstract: Personalized cancer treatment requires stratification of patients based on biomarkers. Despite advances in biomarker-guided therapy, biomarkers are not always available or sufficient to predict treatment responses in individual patients. Functional ex vivo cancer models with the potential to assess therapeutic outcomes upfront have been developed but have not been implemented in clinical practice—despite accumulating evidence of their clinical relevance. This review describes how three essential steps in the development of personalized functional prediction tests (analytical validity, clinical validity, and clinical utility) should be combined in a multidisciplinary approach: Integrated Translational Co-design. This approach front-loads clinical utility and validation constraints into early analytical design decisions, so that biological fidelity, clinical implementation, and healthcare costs can be optimized from the start of assay development.

articles.title: Lipid droplet targeting at single-molecule resolution
articles.abstract: Lipid droplet proteins can move from the endoplasmic reticulum to droplets through persistent membrane connections. A new single-molecule study reveals that accumulation is not only about access: protein sequence features tune residence on the droplet surface, revealing how confined mobility can lead to accumulation on the organelle (Mizrak et al.).

articles.title: Parasites in the meta-ecosystem landscape: hidden connectors and disruptors
articles.abstract: The meta-ecosystem framework explains spatial flows of organisms, materials, and energy across ecosystem boundaries. Parasites play crucial roles in these processes, yet they remain absent from meta-ecosystem models. Using examples from terrestrial and aquatic environments, we illustrate how parasitic organisms act as central connectors or disruptors of the flow of organisms, nutrients, and energy across ecosystem boundaries via four key mechanisms: parasite-induced host movement, behavioural changes that increase cross-ecosystem predation, host mortality, and parasite avoidance behaviour. These examples highlight the central role of parasites in driving and regulating nutrient and energy flow from catchment-to-coast, and we outline a pathway for improved integration of these parasite-mediated processes into the meta-ecosystem framework.

articles.title: Automated generation and execution of large-scale semidefinite programs for variational two-electron reduced density matrix theory
articles.abstract: The variational two-electron reduced density matrix (v2RDM) method provides a wave-function-free approach to the description of strong electron correlation whose computational cost scales polynomially with the number of correlated orbitals. Here, we present an automated pipeline for the generation and execution of semidefinite programs (SDPs) associated with the v2RDM problem. Algebraic constraints encoding ensemble $N$-representability conditions are generated via the p$^\dagger$q second-quantized algebra package, and the p$^\dagger$q-generated expressions are automatically translated into a sparse-matrix representation that can be digested by an appropriate SDP solver. We have implemented a boundary-point SDP (BPSDP) solver in the libsdp package that can execute the v2RDM SDPs on either CPU or GPU hardware. We apply the code in several contexts. First, two-particle conditions are used to describe the 76-orbital model of the iron-molybdenum cofactor (FeMoco) of nitrogenase, the simulation of which requires roughly 25 hours of compute time on a single Nvidia H100 GPU. Second, the performance of high-order (four-particle positivity) conditions is evaluated on a challenging two-dimensional H$_{10}$ cluster problem. Lastly, new classes of positivity constraints for mixed fermion-boson systems are generated and applied within the context of ab initio cavity quantum electrodynamics simulations.

articles.title: Bounds on Attainable Rate Modulation in Fermi's Golden Rule
articles.abstract: Controlling transition rates is a central objective across quantum optics, condensed-matter physics, and chemical physics, encompassing processes such as spontaneous emission, energy and charge transfer, spin relaxation, and chemical reactions. Although Fermi's golden rule provides a powerful framework for calculating such rates of weakly coupled transitions, conventional calculations require the interaction to be specified in advance; the range of rate responses attainable over a broader interaction space remains unknown. We formulate spectral-overlap golden-rule rates as quadratic forms of the interaction and derive rigorous bounds on rate modulation over a specified interaction space. As an example, application to energy transfer from a donor to a molecular vibration coupled to an optical cavity reveals that enhancement and suppression depend jointly on the interaction and cavity detuning, including continuous reversal of the rate response for a fixed interaction. The same approach may elucidate rate control for other golden-rule processes, including excitation-energy transfer, nonadiabatic electron transfer, nonradiative electronic transitions, vibrational and spin relaxation, and spontaneous emission.

articles.title: Choosing Spatial Resolution in the Residence-Time Approach to Local Diffusivity
articles.abstract: Estimating position-dependent diffusivity with the residence-time approach (RTA) requires choosing an interval width that resolves spatial variation while probing time scales compatible with a local diffusion model. We develop a selection criterion that combines bulk diffusivity convergence with local model agreement measured by the Kullback-Leibler divergence between observed and predicted first-exit-time distributions, and assess global model agreement through independent propagator analysis against unbiased molecular dynamics. Applications to water in a fluid phospholipid bilayer and three permeants in a model skin lipid barrier show that local agreement alone does not ensure global fidelity: in the skin barrier, narrow intervals minimize exit-time mismatch but predict excessive spreading, whereas requiring bulk convergence selects wider intervals with better longer-time predictions. In propagator tests, RTA profiles at the selected interval widths outperform velocity-autocorrelation-based profiles and generally improve agreement relative to position-autocorrelation-based profiles in the skin barrier, while phospholipid-bilayer rankings depend on lag time and discrepancy metric; both autocorrelation methods use harmonically restrained simulations.

articles.title: Coherent dynamics and ultrafast evolution of optical nonlinearity of self-hybridized exciton-polaritons in WSe2
articles.abstract: Exciton-polaritons (EPs) are valuable for investigating macroscopic quantum coherent phenomena. However, overcoming the rapid decoherence of EPs under ambient conditions is challenging, even using delicately fabricated optical cavities. Here, we show pronounced coherent dynamics in thin flakes of WSe2 supporting self-hybridized EPs. Ultrafast two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy (2DES) resolves two types of quantum beating: Rabi oscillation with a period of ~ 24 fs and a slower, ~ 50 fs period oscillation, revealing coherent coupling not only between excitons and cavity, but also between polaritons and dark states. Rapid evolution of 2DES line shape indicates a change of dominant optical nonlinearities from Rabi contraction of polaritons to many-body interactions of excitons in the first 100 fs, marking the transition from coherent to incoherent polariton excitations. The results are rationalized by a three-coupled oscillator model considering the inhomogeneous cavity field distribution. We also demonstrate coherent quantum beating between A exciton and its excited Rydberg state A* under ambient conditions. Our results shed light on the coherent control in readily accessible semiconductor thin flakes.

articles.title: Concentration-Dependent Speciation in ZnCl2 Electrolyte Solutions: Transferability of Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials and Speciation Sensitivity of EXAFS
articles.abstract: Predicting speciation in concentrated electrolytes requires accurate ion interactions and adequate sampling of slowly interconverting coordination environments. We combine Zn K-edge extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) measurements with long-timescale molecular dynamics (MD) using machine-learning interatomic potentials to study aqueous ZnCl2 from dilute conditions to 30 m. We train revPBE-based DeepMD models with D3 corrections included or excluded for Zn-containing pairs and compare them with DPMD-SCAN, classical MD (CMD), and MACE-MATPES-r2SCAN. EXAFS calculations are benchmarked against hydrated and chloride-coordinated Zn reference complexes, then applied to MD ensembles alongside Zn-Cl coordination free-energy analysis. Increasing concentration reduces octahedral coordination, replaces water with chloride, and promotes chloride-bridged association. All three DeepMD models yield similar EXAFS at 3 m, but DPMD-SCAN shows greater transferability across concentrations, reproducing measured spectral trends, key features of mixed ZnCl2/LiCl spectra, and octahedral fractions consistent with other studies. DFT treatment strongly affects coordination free energies and aggregation; excluding Zn-related D3 corrections does not systematically improve EXAFS agreement. CMD shows larger spectral discrepancies and less consistent coordination trends. MACE-MATPES-r2SCAN improves upon CMD and yields spectra comparable to DPMD-SCAN, which provides more consistent agreement and greater computational efficiency. Neighbor-resolved analysis shows that distance disorder and scattering-path interference can produce similar EXAFS signatures for distinct coordination ensembles, highlighting the need for rigorous sampling and ensemble-averaged spectra to distinguish isolated from chloride-bridged Zn species.

articles.title: Consistent Modeling of SEI Growth via Electron Diffusion Validated Across Diverse Cell Specifications and Operating Conditions in LFP/Graphite Cells
articles.abstract: Understanding and predicting degradation in lithium-ion batteries is critical for their widespread deployment. The continuous growth of the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) remains a dominant aging pathway, yet accurately modeling its kinetics across diverse cell specifications and operating conditions remains a significant challenge. Here, we present and validate a physically grounded SEI growth model mediated by the electron diffusion mechanism. This framework intrinsically captures the state of charge (SOC) dependence of degradation through the impact of the anode potential on the electron concentration, which governs the rate of SEI growth. The presented model explicitly accounts for variations in electrolyte salt, anode material, temperature, and cycling rate. Validation against experimental aging data for LFP/graphite cells demonstrates high predictive accuracy across a broad range of cell specifications and cycling conditions, including confined SOC windows, electrolyte salts (LiFSI, LiPF6), artificial graphites (AGC, AGD), temperatures (40-70°C), and C-rates (C/20-1C). Remarkably, a single, consistent set of parameters is applied to simulate the capacity fade for all experiments without recalibration. While quantitative overestimations occur during high-SOC storage periods, the framework consistently captures the observed degradation trends. Our findings underscore that lower SOC operation mitigates degradation, establishing a physics-based model for predicting long-term lithium-ion battery aging.

articles.title: Differentiated Determinant Graphs Enable Large-Scale Multideterminant Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo
articles.abstract: Multideterminant trial wave functions can reduce phaseless bias in auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC), but the repeated evaluation of their overlap, force bias, and local energy restricts systematic trial improvement. In this work, we organize particle--hole excitation determinants as a shared arithmetic directed acyclic graph of canonical minors. A coefficient-weighted reverse pass and batched directional passes evaluate the complete estimator without determinant-resolved cofactor tensors while preserving the sparse $α$--$β$ coefficient coupling exactly. Controlled complex-valued tests verify the complete kernel to machine precision and show orders-of-magnitude acceleration over direct determinant summation. In molecular calculations, the observed cost remains sublinear through million-configuration selected-CI trials and the same estimator remains usable at one hundred million configurations, where the eventual exact coefficient-contraction boundary becomes visible. For Cr$_2$, an orbital-optimized CAS(12e,42o) trial in a double-$ζ$ basis yields a potential-energy curve (PEC) and spectroscopic constants in close agreement with experiment. Differentiated determinant graphs therefore convert very large correlated trials from a formal accuracy hierarchy into a practical route for systematic AFQMC studies of strongly correlated molecules.

articles.title: Einstein's theory of Brownian motion: The non-Fickian normal diffusion
articles.abstract: Einstein's theory of diffusion defines what is considered {\it normal diffusion}. Historically, Einstein considered homogeneous diffusion characterised by a diffusion constant in his original calculations, resulting in what is known as {\it Fickian} diffusion, which thermally relaxes concentration inhomogeneities. However, in the same derivation of Einstein, the seed of generalisation of the theory to {\it non-Fickian} diffusion in the presence of space-dependent diffusivity is hidden. This indicates that non-Fickian diffusion, which can drive concentration inhomogeneities, can also be normal diffusion. The present article discusses the origin of the {\it normal} non-Fickian diffusion in Einstein's theory of diffusion.

articles.title: Fast2Peak: High-Fidelity Restoration Algorithm by Single-Pixel Masking towards Real-Time Spectral Measurements
articles.abstract: Improving the temporal and spatial resolution of spectroscopy inevitably reduces the photons available to each measurement, pushing rapid measurements into photon-starved conditions where weak spectral features are obscured by stochastic background noise. Here, we present Fast2Peak (F2P), a self-supervised Transformer framework that transforms the spectral restoration task into a context-prediction problem. Given that physically constrained spectral signals exhibit strong local continuity, whereas the stochastic noise fluctuates randomly and does not possess the continuity across neighboring spectral pixels, single-pixel masking enables F2P to restore the predictable signal structure while suppressing unpredictable fluctuations even without clean reference spectra. Unlike conventional offline spectral restoration, F2P achieves high-fidelity restoration within milliseconds, enabling real-time "acquire-and-process" operation. We demonstrate this capability in time-resolved electrochemical SERS and hyperspectral Raman imaging, where spectral restoration is performed during data acquisition. In addition, F2P has demonstrated its robust generalization across different instruments and spectral modalities, including Raman, NMR, XRD and FTIR.

articles.title: Hierarchical Response Theory of Electronegativity from Atomic Mean Inner Potential
articles.abstract: Electronegativity, introduced by Pauling nearly a century ago, remains chemistry's most widely used yet conceptually ambiguous quantity: is it a fixed atomic constant, or does it depend on chemical environment? We resolve this debate by recasting electronegativity as a continuous response function rooted in the Atomic Mean Inner Potential (AMIP), a quantum-mechanical observable accessible through first-principles calculation and, ultimately, electron holography. Expanding the AMIP with respect to fractional electron removal defines a hierarchy of physically distinct coefficients: the static electronegativity $χ_0$, the Electrostatic Rigidity $\mathcal{R}$---whose sign indicates whether an atom hardens or softens upon oxidation---and the Electrostatic Anharmonic Modulus $\mathcal{A}$. A logarithmic-derivative decomposition links these coefficients to two competing microscopic channels, electronic screening loss and geometric volume collapse, whose balance governs the response of all 102 elements. This competition produces a systematic dichotomy between softening main-group elements and hardening d-block elements, two scaling laws within the transition series (closed-shell stiffening and principal quantum softening), and two anomalies: a pronounced exchange-driven effect at half-filled d$^{5}$ configurations and a near-perfect cancellation in Ce. It also resolves the long-standing Cs--Fr controversy, identifying Fr as a critical element whose near-boundary response is amplified fivefold by relativistic contraction of the 7s orbital. The framework reproduces the classical Allen, Pauling, and Mulliken scales as well as Lewis acidity trends, and makes three falsifiable experimental predictions. It transforms electronegativity from a lookup-table number into a predictive, hierarchically structured quantum descriptor.

articles.title: Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (MQE): A Selective State Space Model for Scalable Ground State Simulations in Quantum Chemistry
articles.abstract: Predicting molecular electronic structure using Quantum Computing approaches is a challenge in Computational Chemistry. Traditional Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) are typically hindered by optimization challenges. The alternative Generative Quantum Eigensolver (GQE) mitigates this by reformulating ground-state search as discrete sequence generation, but its Transformer backbone suffers from quadratic computational complexity, bottlenecking scalability for larger molecules. To address this, we introduce the Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (Mamba-QE), which replaces the Transformer with a Selective State Space Model (SSM) to process operator sequences with linear $\mathcal{O}(L)$ complexity. Additionally, we integrate a distance-conditioned mechanism enabling the direct prediction of complete potential energy surfaces (PES). Evaluated on the $H_2$ molecule, Mamba-QE reproduces Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) reference energies well within chemical accuracy, achieving an energy error below $3\times10^{-6}$ Ha across 16 geometries with zero variational violations. Mamba-QE maintains high expressive power while establishing a robust, scalable foundation for quantum simulations of complex molecular systems.

articles.title: Methane and ethane adsorption on calcite surfaces: effects of surface morphology from molecular dynamics and 3D-RISM
articles.abstract: Understanding the adsorption of alkanes on mineral surfaces is important for industrial processes such as oil and gas recovery from shale reservoirs. Previous studies have examined the adsorption of functionalized and non-functionalized alkanes on calcite, as well as adsorption under confinement. However, real surfaces commonly exhibit defects that can influence adsorption behavior. In this work, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and the three-dimensional reference interaction site model (3D-RISM) are used to investigate the adsorption of methane and ethane on calcite surfaces with step defects. MD simulations were carried out with and without positional restraints to investigate the effects of carbonate reorientation. 3D-RISM calculations were performed on these structures and on energy-minimized configurations of the relaxed crystal. Both methods show adsorption enhanced at step defects relative to flat regions, with methane exhibiting higher excess adsorption than ethane. Carbonate reorientation at the relaxed step edges reduces the local density peaks at specific step sites in both methods, while the integrated excess adsorption from MD remains comparable to that of the restrained surface. 3D-RISM predicts lower maxima for the highest density peaks and larger excess adsorption than MD, but reproduces the spatial organization and overall adsorption trends at a fraction of the computational cost. These results highlight the importance of surface heterogeneity in fluid-mineral interactions and demonstrate that 3D-RISM is an efficient tool for semi-quantitative screening of adsorption across complex surface geometries

articles.title: Photon Correlations Control Quantum Fisher Information in Coherent Multidimensional Spectroscopy
articles.abstract: Coherent multidimensional spectroscopy probes interactions and dynamics of molecular systems through nonlinear optical signals. Quantum light excitation has been explored as a means of controlling these signals, raising the question of how excitation-light correlations affect the precision of molecular parameter estimation from the emitted signal. In this work, we show that photon-number correlations and two-photon coherence play distinct roles in encoding molecular information in the emitted rephasing signal. In the weak-emission regime and within the single Schmidt pair approximation, we derive a normally ordered information law in which the joint photon-number moment and the squared magnitude of the two-photon coherence weight the amplitude and phase sensitivities of the molecular response, respectively. For matched temporal modes and mean photon numbers in each input mode, two-mode squeezed vacuum enhances both weights relative to coherent excitation, whereas independent displaced squeezing preserves the amplitude weight but reduces the phase weight. The background population and its parameter dependence also affect the total quantum Fisher information, which therefore cannot be inferred from the coherent mean-field signal alone. We derive a leading-order bound on its enhancement over coherent excitation when the background population is nonnegative and common to the compared sources. These findings provide criteria for selecting excitation sources according to how the target molecular parameter affects the amplitude and phase of the response.

articles.title: QuDPy-FDGF: A Python-Based Tool for Computing Ultrafast Nonlinear Optical Responses Using Frequency Domain Green's Functions
articles.abstract: We present QuDPy-FDGF, an open-source Python framework that evaluates Liouville-space pathways as hybrid chains of time propagators and frequency-domain Green's functions. Frequency-resolved intervals are computed directly through shifted linear systems, without time propagation followed by a Fourier transform, while other intervals may remain in the time domain. A model-agnostic block interface separates the physical model from pathway construction, numerical propagation, and detection. The released implementation provides an explicit dense Liouville-space backend for reference calculations and a sector-resolved sparse backend using matrix-free generator actions, Krylov time propagation, and generalized minimal residual (GMRES) resolvent solves. Its observable layer reuses propagated pathway responses to evaluate operator expectation values, action-detected readout interactions, instantaneous jump rates, and integrated mean jump counts. The framework is assessed on an analytically solvable open two-level system and on two examples of increasing complexity: the complete third-order rephasing response, with its eight sequences, of a thermally initialized anisotropic Heisenberg (XXZ) spin chain with unequal excitation sectors, and two coupled dissipative anharmonic modes whose spectra depend on the detected observable, with the fifth-order double-quantum response of their closed limit. The calculations reproduce the analytical two-level response, check the matrix-free sparse evaluation against the dense assembly of the generator, and recover the harmonic-limit cancellation of the fifth-order signal when the required three-excitation manifold is retained. QuDPy-FDGF therefore provides a unified framework for pathway- and observable-resolved nonlinear spectroscopy in finite or truncated Hilbert spaces with unitary or Markovian Gorini--Kossakowski--Sudarshan--Lindblad (GKSL) dynamics.

articles.title: SU(2)-Equivariant Spinor Message Passing for Molecular Magnetism
articles.abstract: Predicting molecular magnetic properties often requires costly electronic-structure calculations that account for spin-orbit coupling. Inspired by the spinor nature of the underlying electronic states, we introduce eSpinor, an SU(2)-equivariant graph neural network that propagates spinor features alongside the integer-rank tensors used in conventional equivariant models. We initialize spinors from eigenvectors of an approximate Hamiltonian that includes spin-orbit coupling. The network preserves their rotation laws and makes predictions independent of arbitrary eigenbasis choices. Comparisons with geometry-only and Hamiltonian-informed baselines assess the benefit of this architecture beyond supplying electronic information. On cobalt single-molecule magnet candidates, eSpinor improves magnetic anisotropy predictions, including for unseen ligands. It also improves excitation-energy predictions for dysprosium candidates with unseen ligands, extending the benefit to rotationally invariant scalar targets. For a dysprosium magnetic resonance imaging probe, it predicts real electron-spin correlations and low-field nuclear relaxation rates more accurately despite static crystal-field errors similar to the Hamiltonian-informed baseline. This dynamical advantage extends from water to methanol without retraining. These results support spinor message passing as a useful inductive bias for molecular magnetism in the tested systems and show why model selection should be guided by accuracy on the intended physical observables.

articles.title: Spin-Adapted Spin-Flip Tamm-Dancoff Approximation (XSF-TDA) for Singlet-Triplet Gaps in MR-TADF and INVEST Emitters
articles.abstract: In this work, we assess the recently introduced spin-adapted TDA for spin-flip-down excitations (XSF-TDA) [Mol. Phys. e2631735 (2026)] as a practical approach to this problem. Starting from a high-spin restricted open-shell Kohn--Sham reference, XSF-TDA generates spin-adapted low-spin roots arising from open--open (OO), core--open (CO), open--virtual (OV), and core--virtual (CV) types of spin-flip-down excitations. Across four application sets comprising 243 benchmark cases, XSF-TDA substantially reduces the systematic positive bias observed for TDA and unrestricted spin-flip TDA (USF-TDA). With the B3LYP functional, XSF-TDA reduces the equal-set-weighted macro-MAE relative to USF-TDA from 0.252 eV (0.158 eV) to 0.102~eV (0.056~eV) with the ALDA0 (multicollinear) kernel. Its accuracy is competitive with state-specific $Δ$DFT and quasiparticle-energy DFT (QE-DFT), while being able to provide deeper mechanistic insight through the response vector. In particular, spin-adapted CV configurations provide selected higher-excitation character that strengthens the OO--CV dynamical-spin-polarization channel, which preferentially stabilizes the singlet states. We also identify an INVEST emitter with appreciable OO--OV mixing, suggesting a possible additional contribution to singlet stabilization when the CV contribution is small. The XSF-TDA method therefore provides practical singlet--triplet gap predictions together with interpretable state analysis for the screening and mechanistic understanding of MR-TADF and INVEST emitters.

articles.title: Stationarity Constraints Improve Both Energies and Densities of Machine-Learned Exchange-Correlation Functionals
articles.abstract: Empirical exchange-correlation functionals are fitted on fixed orbitals but used self-consistently, so better energies often come with worse densities. We show that the Brillouin residual of a trained functional on the Kohn-Sham orbitals of an accurate density controls, to first order, both the self-consistent density shift and the gap between fitted and self-consistent energies. Penalizing it requires no self-consistent-field solution during training. Trained on 6 energies and 11 CCSD densities, a neural meta-GGA surpasses SCAN in both atomization energies and densities of unseen molecules.

articles.title: Synthetic Stochastic Time Series from Generative Models
articles.abstract: Obtaining statistically converged time-series data represents a fundamental challenge in computational chemistry, where sampling is constrained by the prohibitive computational cost of high-fidelity simulations. The accuracy attainable from a finite simulation budget is governed by the standard-error scaling $1/\sqrt{n}$, rendering exhaustive sampling challenging for systems of realistic complexity. Here we show that generative models trained on high-quality stochastic trajectories can reproduce key statistical properties of the underlying process and generate additional synthetic trajectories at substantially lower computational cost, thereby enhancing the sampling accessible from a finite set of simulations. We present a systematic comparison of four generative architectures across two complementary data sources: an analytically tractable Ornstein-Uhlenbeck reference and donor-acceptor energy-gap trajectories from all-atom molecular dynamics simulations. Among the four architectures tested, the denoising diffusion probabilistic model reproduces the target statistics most consistently, across both data sources and across the range of correlation times examined, and generates far faster than the sequential Transformer. Specifically, for the energy-gap trajectories, augmentation from 0.1 ns of training data yields statistical estimates comparable in accuracy to those obtained from 0.25-0.50 ns of direct MD sampling. We further show that the benefit of synthetic augmentation is bounded by the information contained in the training data, producing a quality floor determined by both the training data and the generative model. Our findings establish diffusion-based generative models as an effective route to data-driven augmentation of stochastic time series in computational chemistry.

articles.title: Tuning Thermal Memory and Dissipation in Colloidal Glasses via Microgel Particle Stiffness
articles.abstract: The Kovacs effect, characterized by nonlinear, path-dependent structural recovery, is a hallmark of glassy systems. In soft colloidal microgel glasses, the stiffness of the constituent particles governs their deformation, swelling, rearrangement, and response to external stimuli, thereby dictating the path-dependent structural recovery of these jammed non-equilibrium systems. To investigate this influence, microgels of different stiffnesses were synthesized by adjusting the concentration of the polar crosslinker, N, N'-methylenebisacrylamide (MBA). The relaxation of the storage and loss moduli was measured using oscillatory rheology under diverse temperature ramp rates, and cryo-FESEM imaging provided direct visualization of the underlying particle packing. While the rapid adaptability of soft particles and the kinetic arrest of stiff ones suppresses Kovacs asymmetry, intermediate-stiffness particles exhibit moderate thermoresponsivity, traversing distinct energy landscapes on heating and cooling to maximize asymmetry and dissipation. Cryo-FESEM micrographs, displaying gel-like networks in soft particle suspensions, dense packing in stiff particle suspensions, and disordered, compact structures in intermediate-stiffness systems, corroborate these findings. Our results demonstrate that intermediate-stiffness PNIPAM microgels optimize structural recovery, rendering them promising candidates for forming colloidal glasses and establishing Kovacs asymmetry as a robust probe of non-equilibrium dynamics in glassy systems.

articles.title: A mechanistic theory of planning in prefrontal cortex
articles.abstract: Planning is critical for adaptive behaviour in a changing world, because it lets us anticipate the future and adjust our actions accordingly. While prefrontal cortex is crucial for this process, it remains unknown how planning is implemented in neural circuits. Prefrontal representations were recently discovered in simpler sequence memory tasks, where different populations of neurons represent different future time points.
