Retracing the olive (Olea europaea L. subsp. europaea) origin and its early history diffusion among the civilizations overlooking the Mediterranean coasts: an integrated approach
articles.abstract: The olive tree is one of the most important crops in the world, but even more, one of the most identitarian plant for the countries of the Mediterranean basin. In this article, the vast consultation of scientific literature, archaeological, historical and anecdotal sources, allowed to outline a global reasoned vision on the olive origin, its spread during early history and how olive fruit fly may represent as proxy for tracing its early diffusion. The reconstruction of the first forms of exploitation, propagation and trade routes yielded a chronologically coherent westward emergence of integrated olive-oil economies and cultures throughout the Mediterranean Basin, with the exception of some independent cultivation events tied to the widespread diffusion of the wild olive tree from the end of the last Glacial Period. Written sources, iconography, and archaeological installations further anchor this spatio-temporal narrative, leading to the transition from -wild- olives gatherers to olive growers.

articles.title: Correction to ‘Differential effects of pollen nutritional quality on male and female reproductive success within a diverse co‐flowering community’
The effect of prenatal environment on brain mitochondrial function and prey detection in a lizard
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract The ability to detect prey is crucial for survival in many animals. However, prey detection is a cognitive process that can be influenced by early life conditions such as prenatal stress or temperature. Mitochondrial function is likely to underlie these effects because cognitive abilities are energetically demanding (i.e. dependent on efficient metabolic function) and because metabolic‐derived oxidative stress and oxidative damage can impair cognitive function. Yet, whether prenatal stress and thermal environments affect prey detection, and whether mitochondrial function mediates such effects, remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the links between prenatal environments, mitochondrial function and prey detection in the delicate skink (Lampropholis delicata). We manipulated egg corticosterone (CORT) levels—a key stress hormone in reptiles—and incubation temperature and assessed the ability of lizards to detect chemical and visual prey stimuli. Then, using flow cytometry, we measured metabolic function, oxidative stress and oxidative damage in the olfactory bulbs and optic tecta, two brain regions involved in sensory processing. While metabolic function and oxidative stress remained robust to early life conditions, CORT and temperature interacted to influence oxidative damage. Particularly, CORT decreased DNA damage in the olfactory bulbs of cold‐incubated lizards but had no effect on hot‐incubated lizards. In both brain regions, lipid peroxidation was lower in CORT‐treated lizards incubated at high temperatures compared to CORT‐treated cold‐incubated lizards, but no other between‐treatment differences were detected. Additionally, CORT‐treated lizards responded faster when presented with chemical cues but not visual stimuli. We did not find any relationship between mitochondrial function and prey detection. Our findings suggest that prenatal conditions have lasting effects on DNA damage and prey detection, but prey detection appears decoupled from mitochondrial function in L. delicata. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.

articles.title: Phenological Flexibility in Nesting Grassland Birds Over a Half Century Informs Timing of Management
articles.abstract: The timing of biological events for wildlife species reflects and influences ecological and evolutionary processes and helps guide management actions to meet conservation objectives. Climate change may cause phenological shifts across trophic levels and ecosystems, which can have broad ecological impacts. Shifts may also result in mistiming between management practices based on historical conditions and current biological events, reducing the effectiveness of natural resource management and conservation efforts. We analyzed nesting phenology patterns over recent decades across North America for 44 species of grassland‐nesting birds, including waterfowl, upland gamebirds, shorebirds, and passerines, many of which have experienced precipitous population declines. Understanding nesting phenologies of these species is important to their conservation, as grassland management activities often conflict with reproductive periods leading to high nest and young mortality. We compiled a dataset of over 172,000 nest records spanning five decades and evaluated environmental factors influencing long‐term shifts and short‐term flexibility in nesting phenology. We found considerable variation in responses among species, with differences in both direction and magnitude of spatiotemporal effects on nest initiation dates. Notably, the community‐level nesting season lengthened over time, but shifts exhibited spatial heterogeneity within this community of grassland birds. Nesting dates shifted asymmetrically across the breeding season with differential changes in early, peak, and late nesting dates whereas long‐term changes were mediated by weather and geographic gradients. For example, nest initiation was earlier in warmer and wetter years. By applying a quantile‐based analysis, we provide estimates of the full nesting period that could serve as a flexible tool for scheduling monitoring efforts and balancing management and human activities with periods of reduced nesting activity. Our collaborative effort illustrates the challenges and opportunities of collecting long‐term data on avian communities necessary for answering questions across large regions but highlights the value of research coordination for bird conservation.

articles.title: Skin-resident CXCR6+ memory CD4+ T cells and dendritic cells form dermal perivascular hubs that drive relapse in allergic dermatitis
articles.abstract: Tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells are heterogeneous, but how pathogenic subsets drive relapse in allergic dermatitis remains unclear. Asahina et al. identify a pathogenic CXCR6+ CD4+ TRM subset sustained through CXCL16-dependent clustering with CD301b+ cDC2s, revealing the TRM-DC niche as a potential therapeutic target for allergic dermatitis.

articles.title: Cost effectiveness of synthetic fuel and CO2 removal for net-zero aviation
articles.abstract: Aviation's climate impact goes beyond CO2, yet current policies such as the EU's ReFuelEU regulation push almost exclusively toward sustainable fuels, overlooking an alternative: permanently capturing CO2 from the air via DACCS while continuing to burn fossil jet fuel. Comparing long-term costs of both approaches, we find DACCS is 49%–69% cheaper than synthetic fuels and needs far less renewable electricity, suggesting that current policy may be locking aviation into a costlier decarbonization path than necessary.

articles.title: High-frequency inductively heated molten salt bubbling beds for methane pyrolysis
articles.abstract: Methane pyrolysis can produce hydrogen while sequestering solid carbon, but efficient high-grade heat delivery and coking management remain challenging. This study shows that high-frequency magnetic induction directly and volumetrically heats molten salt bubbling beds with stable power delivery, providing a scalable route for methane pyrolysis while managing solid carbon formation. These principles have applicability more broadly to molten salt chemical conversion and thermal energy storage systems.

articles.title: Host‐mediated filtering and interspecific associations structure strongyle parasite communities in Sable Island horses
articles.abstract: Using individual‐level nemabiome metabarcoding of 3147 samples from 916 horses on Sable Island over 10 years, we generate the largest dataset of its kind to date. This unprecedented scale enables a rare test of the processes structuring parasite communities in a natural system, revealing dominant host‐mediated filtering and predominantly positive species associations. Abstract Mixed‐species parasite infections are common in wildlife, yet the ecological processes that structure these communities remain poorly understood. We hypothesized that host‐mediated and extrinsic environmental filtering, alongside biotic interactions, act concurrently to shape parasite community composition, and that these structuring patterns would depend on parasite traits or evolutionary history. We applied nemabiome DNA metabarcoding to 3147 faecal samples from 916 feral horses with no history of anthelmintic treatment, collected over 10 years as part of a long‐term individual‐based study on Sable Island, Canada. Using joint species distribution models, we tested whether strongyle parasite communities were structured by host‐associated factors, extrinsic environmental variables or interspecific interactions. Host factors, particularly age and individual identity, explained the greatest proportion of variation in both parasite prevalence and infection intensity, indicating strong host‐mediated environmental filtering. In contrast, spatial location and year explained minimal variation, suggesting weaker effects of extrinsically mediated environmental filtering. Parasite traits such as body size and gut site preference had limited associations with species' environmental responses. Positive species associations were common, particularly among species occupying the same gut region, suggesting that strong, consistent competitive interactions were not prominently reflected in the residual covariance structure. Negative associations were less frequent but consistently involved Strongylus equinus, indicating potential context‐dependent biotic interactions involving this species. By integrating species‐level molecular data with hierarchical joint species models, this study quantifies patterns of host‐related filtering and species co‐variation within a natural parasite community and provides a framework for examining mixed infections in wild systems.

articles.title: Design and engineering of a sustainable, reusable Fe@ISCOF SPE catalyst with suppressed metal leaching for electro-organic Reppe sulfonation enabling efficient synthesis of phenylethane-1-sulfonate derivatives in DES matrix
Ground‐penetrating radar amplitudes to roots: A numerical modelling framework for mapping coarse root system architecture
articles.abstract: Observations of three‐dimensional (3D) coarse root system architecture remain limited because most measurement approaches require excavation. Here, we combined dense single‐ and multi‐channel 500 MHz ground‐penetrating radar (GPR) surveys with a flow‐guided connectivity framework to non‐destructively characterise the coarse root architecture of two trees. Migrated and depth‐normalised GPR amplitudes were treated as spatially variable hydraulic conductivities in a steady‐state numerical model. The resulting connectivity fields transformed spatially discontinuous, collapsed diffraction hyperbolae into continuous 3D representations of root architecture extending 10–15 m from the trunk. We applied this approach to a swamp oak (Quercus palustris) and a river red gum (Eucalyptus camaldulensis). The two trees were surveyed under different environmental conditions and acquisition parameters. The reconstructed architectures revealed shallow, laterally extensive coarse root systems and captured substantial variation in root structure between the two trees. The oak roots exhibited an asymmetrical architecture with preferential development towards the upslope, wind‐exposed side of the tree, whereas the river red gum displayed a more radially distributed root architecture with deeper roots near the trunk. Approximately 80% of reconstructed roots for both trees occurred within 6.2 m of the trunk and above 60 cm depth. Together, these results demonstrate that dense GPR surveys, coupled with connectivity‐based modelling, provide a non‐destructive and repeatable approach for characterising coarse root architecture.

articles.title: UNIQAT: An open‐source toolkit for reproducible image quality assessment in marine surveys
articles.abstract: Modern marine surveys generate tens of thousands of underwater images per expedition, yet many are unusable due to image quality deterioration. Manual quality screening is labour-intensive, subjective and inconsistent across observers and teams, hindering reproducible science, creating large backlogs of unprocessed imagery, and limiting real-time algorithmic and robotic applications. We present UNIQAT (UNderwater Image Quality Assessment Toolkit), an open-source Python toolkit for automated underwater image quality assessment. The toolkit computes reference-free quality metrics across nine categories of image characteristics relevant to underwater images, such as colour cast, turbidity and contrast loss. Metrics can be combined with user-defined weights into task-specific quality scores tailored to different ecological applications. High-performance computing (HPC)-aware multiprocessing and optional deep learning architectures for metric approximation support processing at scales matching modern survey data collection. We evaluated UNIQAT on 130,845 images from nine coral reef surveys conducted by the Australian Institute of Marine Science; every result reported in the main text was produced by the traditional metrics pipeline, with no deep learning model involved, and a separate training demonstration is reported in the Supporting Information. The traditional metrics pipeline, run as 48 CPU workers on a 64-core cluster node, processed 7.9 4K-images/s, with processing time scaling linearly with image count (r 2 = 0.98). The resulting quality scores captured expected patterns of image modulation based on the environmental context of the imaged scenes: All nine surveys showed negative depth–quality correlations (r = −0.16 to −0.89), consistent with the depth-dependent deterioration of image quality in underwater environments. Cross-survey metric profiles were highly consistent (mean Spearman ρ = 0.99 across all 36 pairwise comparisons, minimum 0.96), confirming measurement stability across different dates, locations, camera systems and environmental conditions. Synthesis. UNIQAT can help deliver objective and tunable image quality metrics in a versatile toolkit that enables transparent reporting and supports unsupervised quality assessment for applications in marine monitoring and robotics.

articles.title: A CK2-β-TrCP kinase-E3 ubiquitin ligase cascade is a metabolic sensor regulating tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase stability
articles.abstract: How metabolic enzyme levels are regulated is poorly understood. Studying the tryptophan (Trp)-metabolizing enzyme TDO2, Thielen et al. discover a CK2 kinase-β-TrCP E3 ligase pathway that regulates stability in response to substrate availability. Trp occupation of an exosite restricts degron accessibility, whereas low Trp releases the degron for phosphorylation-ubiquitylation-mediated degradation.

articles.title: PHYHD1-mediated translational control regulates renal cell carcinoma progression
articles.abstract: Liang et al. identify phytanoyl-CoA dioxygenase domain containing 1 (PHYHD1) as a tumor suppressor that regulates protein production in kidney cancer. Loss of PHYHD1 promotes disease progression by increasing ceramide transporter 1 (CERT1) production, uncovering a regulatory pathway that may help predict patient outcomes and provide a therapeutic opportunity for PHYHD1-deficient tumors.

articles.title: Advancing Marine Mammal Conservation Through Omics Tools and Integration of Indigenous Ecological Knowledge
articles.abstract: Conservation of biodiversity is a global priority as human‐driven pressures continue to intensify and alter ecosystems worldwide. Marine mammals are vulnerable species, facing numerous escalating anthropogenic threats. Here, we evaluate how, as omics technologies become more accessible and affordable, established and emerging tools are advancing effective marine mammal research and conservation management. Assessments of genetic diversity, adaptive capacity, demographic history and local adaptation provide vital insights into how marine mammal populations respond to environmental change across contemporary and evolutionary timescales. Whole‐genome sequencing, functional genomics, epigenetics and multi‐omic integration enable deeper insights into the molecular basis of complex fitness‐related traits. Approaches like epigenetics, ancient DNA and environmental DNA offer new opportunities to study cryptic, rare, or historical populations and evolutionary processes. Yet, effective marine mammal conservation management cannot rely exclusively on increased availability of omics tools and data. We emphasize the need and obligation for genuine collaboration and integration of Indigenous perspectives with marine mammal genomics approaches to foster ethical, inclusive and effective conservation, and suggest best practices for this. Additionally, we highlight that translating omics data into practical conservation outcomes remains challenging, requiring clear communication, collaboration and integration into management. Using marine mammal genomics to address conservation challenges in a changing world requires innovation, partnership and the integration of diverse knowledge systems, such as Indigenous Ecological Knowledge.

articles.title: Chilling Injury to Algal Symbionts Induces Host Starvation and Metabolic Reorganization in a Temperate Cnidarian
articles.abstract: Global temperature anomalies increasingly disrupt the cnidarian‐algal symbiosis resulting in a phenomenon termed bleaching. In contrast to heat stress, the mechanisms underlying symbiotic breakdown under cold stress remain largely unknown. Combining physiological and metabolomic measurements, we investigated the response of the photosymbiotic sea anemone holobiont Aiptasia couchii to an experiment mimicking a cold spell in the Mediterranean Sea. Within 4 weeks, we observed the onset of symbiotic breakdown reflected in reduced algal endosymbiont density and chlorophyll a content. While photosynthetic efficiency remained largely unaffected, no gross photosynthesis was detectable in cold‐stressed anemones and decreases in glycosyldiacylglycerols and fatty acyl glycosides indicated chloroplast lipid remobilization. This breakdown of symbiotic carbon cycling was reflected in increased dipeptide and ceramide levels suggesting anemones catabolized protein reserves and induced pre‐apoptotic pathways. Taken together, these responses suggest a decoupling of light and dark reactions of photosynthesis in cold‐stressed endosymbionts, resembling chilling injury in higher plants and free‐living microalgae. This chilling‐induced collapse of symbiotic nutrient cycling eventually leads to host starvation in cold‐stressed Cnidaria. Hence, while cold and heat stress may invoke contrasting physiological effects on endosymbionts, our results suggest that both stressors destabilize the symbiosis through similar mechanisms culminating in host starvation.

articles.title: Host‐Associated Differentiation in a Parasitoid Wasp Connected to Venom‐Related but Not Chemosensory Genes
articles.abstract: The mechanisms driving the megadiversity of parasitic wasps remain a central question in evolutionary ecology. To investigate the genomic architecture underlying host‐associated differentiation in parasitic wasps, we generated a de novo genome assembly and performed whole‐genome re‐sequencing of 17 populations of the parasitoid wasp Asecodes parviclava (Eulophidae) across a latitudinal gradient and multiple Galerucella host species. Despite panmixia in host populations, we identified three genetically differentiated wasp lineages, with the most profound divergence separating Galerucella tenella‐associated wasps from other populations. Locus‐specific scans revealed that selection acts highly asymmetrically. We detected significant differentiation and copy‐number expansion clustered within venom‐related gene families, contrasting sharply with a near‐complete lack of divergence in chemosensory genes. This decoupled evolution suggests that host finding may rely on behavioural plasticity, whereas physiological compatibility is genetically hard‐wired via multi‐layered immune‐suppression mechanisms. Finally, asymmetrical gene flow in northern populations demonstrates that fine‐scale habitat overlap creates ecological connectivity without eroding specialized lineages, as intense host‐mediated selection purges maladapted hybrids. Ultimately, our study demonstrates that physiological barriers, rather than behavioural recognition, may maintain specialized parasitoid lineages, providing new insights into the genomic basis of speciation with gene flow in specialized natural enemies.

articles.abstract: After more than 33 years, NASA’s Astrophysics Data System will close its virtual doors in November 2026 and be replaced by its much-expanded successor, Science Explorer. While the core functionality and astrophysics database will remain the same, SciX will extend its relevance to a broader range of scientists.

articles.title: Transitioning from ADS to SciX to serve twenty-first century astronomy
articles.abstract: For decades, the NASA Astrophysics Data System (ADS) has been the foundational digital library for astronomy. As ADS now becomes the Science Explorer (SciX), the team prioritizes preserving this trusted experience while increasing their support for space and Earth sciences more broadly, without diluting its commitment to astrophysics.

articles.title: Gas-diffusion electrode meets plasma
articles.abstract: Efforts to improve carbon dioxide electroreduction have often focused on the catalyst. Now, by focusing on the gas instead, non-thermal plasma activation can unlock products that are not accessible through conventional electrocatalysis.

articles.title: Zbtb44-mediated transcriptional repression critically regulates colonic inflammation
articles.abstract: Poojary and colleagues show that the transcription factor Zbtb44 suppresses colonic inflammation and epithelial cell damage by deregulated T cells.

articles.title: Molecular weaving goes multilevel
articles.abstract: Integrating distinct weaving topologies within a single molecular network creates coupled deformation modes and adaptive adsorption behaviour, pointing to a shift from constructing molecular topologies to exploiting them for functions.

articles.title: A health-system-scale, episode-resolved multimodal atlas of cancer cachexia
articles.abstract: Cancer cachexia is a wasting syndrome with outsized impact on morbidity and mortality, yet its drivers and systemic consequences remain poorly defined. In this study, we repurposed longitudinal clinicogenomic data from 52,236 patients with cancer profiled by MSK-IMPACT (2010–2024) at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center to define episode-resolved trajectories of consensus-defined cachectic weight loss and linked these events to outcomes, serology and tumor genotypes. Cachectic episodes clustered near periods of disease progression and were associated with inferior outcomes in nearly all cancer types. Across diverse malignancies, cachectic weight loss episodes exhibited a consistent serologic signature characterized by lower albumin and hemoglobin and higher levels of liver enzymes. Numerous somatic tumor genotypes, including TP53 mutation across several diseases, were also associated with more frequent onset of cachectic episodes. Motivated by these observations, we developed a multivariate model to predict impending risk of cachectic weight loss in patients with lung, colorectal and prostate cancer, validated in an independent, external cohort from Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (n = 5,785). Routine clinicogenomic data are, therefore, a scalable resource for discovery in cancer cachexia. Using longitudinal data from 52,236 patients with cancer, this study created a multimodal atlas of cancer cachexia, demonstrating that weight loss episodes are linked to systemic serologic signatures and specific tumor genotypes and can be predicted using integrated clinical and molecular data, enabling earlier identification.

articles.title: Population-scale reconstruction of menopause dynamics reveals a physiological cliff at the final menstrual period
articles.abstract: By using a novel computational framework, a cross-sectional analysis on laboratory data from two independent cohorts reveals that the final menstrual period marks an abrupt, multisystem physiological shift, with sex hormone changes beginning more than 10 years before menopause onset.

articles.title: Early-career balancing act: training, moving, relationships and language learning
articles.abstract: These early career scientists in Europe share challenges and advice about finding the ‘right’ lab and lab–life blend.

articles.title: Alus harbor genetic variants that shape the human cortex
articles.abstract: The genetic changes associated with development of the human cortex are difficult to test functionally, especially in the context of gene regulation. In this issue, Matoba et al. show that variants that shape human cortical structure are hiding inside Alu transposable elements, co-opting their inbuilt machinery to rewire regulatory networks in the developing brain.

articles.title: Genome-wide analysis of common structural variants in Alzheimer’s disease identifies a risk-associated regulatory CCG repeat in FAM193B
articles.abstract: This study identifies common structural variants contributing to Alzheimer’s disease heritability. An expanded promoter CCG repeat increases FAM193B expression and disease risk, linking its expression to DNA damage and cell death pathways in neurons.

articles.title: Investigating molecular and hemodynamic effects of LSD in the human brain
articles.abstract: Using simultaneous PET–MRI, McCulloch, Larsen and colleagues quantify LSD’s dose–occupancy relationship at the serotonin 2A receptor and reveal hemodynamic effects of LSD that contrast with those of psilocybin.

articles.title: Chip-mediated manipulation of photonic quantum skyrmions
articles.abstract: Although photonic quantum skyrmions can be generated as entangled or single-photon states, a means to switch between the two is required for quantum information processing. Now, entangled skyrmions and their manipulation on chip is realized.

articles.title: Morphogenesis of a stratified cell mound at a vortex defect
articles.abstract: In cell monolayers with a vortex-like orientation defect, cells converge towards the core of the defect and form a highly organized three-dimensional mound. This mechanism may be relevant for morphogenesis and tumorigenesis.

articles.title: Filling the massive AI drug discovery data gap
articles.abstract: Charlotte Deane, co-leader of the OpenBind initiative, discusses the need for more protein–small molecule binding data.

articles.title: One-step skeletal editing of oxetanes to thietanes using thiourea
articles.abstract: Four-membered heterocycles are privileged scaffolds in medicinal chemistry, yet valuable thietanes remain underexplored compared with widely studied oxetanes and azetidines. Now a one-step skeletal editing strategy is reported that directly converts oxetanes into thietanes using thiourea.

articles.title: Photocatalytic tetrapeptides for enantioselective visible light-induced transformations
articles.abstract: Research on enantioselective photocatalysis has so far been focused on molecular photocatalysts or large yet easily adaptable photoenzymes. However, both catalysis classes display deficiencies either due to their limited adaptability or their high molecular weight. Here we show that small peptides can bridge the gap between the currently used photocatalysts by combining structural flexibility and low molecular weight. We constructed a small peptide that displays a pyroglutamic acid at its N terminus for substrate recognition. At the C terminus, a thioxanthone-based amino acid was installed to harvest photons and to act catalytically by energy transfer. Two amino acids were sufficient to link the two components, resulting in a photocatalytically active tetrapeptide that was used both for photochemical deracemization and enantioselective [2 + 2] photocycloaddition reactions. Our results demonstrate that small peptides with a molecular weight below 750 Da can act as efficient molecular catalysts for enantioselective photochemical transformations.

articles.title: Scrambling-free synthesis of heteroleptic silylium ions by halide abstraction from halosilanes
articles.abstract: Heteroleptic silylium ions with different substituents at the silicon atom are generally not accessible using established tools for producing such reactive intermediates because substituent exchange reactions occur in acidic media, leading to homoleptic silylium ions with three identical alkyl and aryl substituents, respectively. Here we report a broadly applicable route to heteroleptic silylium ions using halosilanes as silylium ion precursors, which are less prone to that scrambling process. While this deceptively simple method has failed so far owing to the lack of a suitable halide-abstracting agent, superhalophilic halogen-substituted silylium ions enable smooth halide abstraction from a diverse set of halosilanes at ambient temperature without substituent redistribution. Accordingly, this approach provides access to essentially any heteroleptic acyclic as well as cyclic silylium-ion motif from common halosilanes, including trialkyl-, dialkyl(aryl)-, alkyldiaryl- and triaryl-substituted congeners. Computational calculations reveal the mechanism of heteroleptic silylium-ion formation and the origin of the suppressed substituent-scrambling process.

Molecular mechanism of KRAS binding to BRAF and its regulation by the BRAF-specific region
articles.abstract: Bonsor et al. determined the crystal structure of the KRAS-BRAF(RBD-CRD) complex, revealing reduced KRAS engagement by BRAF(CRD) compared with CRAF(CRD). They further show that the BRAF-specific region (BSR) attenuates RBD binding to KRAS, while inclusion of the CRD partially relieves this inhibition.

articles.title: [Comment] Hepatitis C—is discrimination preventing elimination?
articles.abstract: The UK (chiefly driven by England and Scotland) is expected to be the first country to meet WHO's goal for the elimination of hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection by 2030. In April, 2026, the UK Health Security Agency's analysis of progress by the National Health Service (NHS) towards elimination showed that 84·6% of people living with HCV had been diagnosed and prevalence in people who inject drugs had fallen to 5·2% in 2024, with an estimated incidence of 4·4 infections per 100 person-years, predicted to fall below WHO's target of two infections per 100 patient-years by 2030.

articles.title: [Comment] Tailoring levels of evidence in trials comparing common treatments
articles.abstract: In many disease settings, physicians and patients can choose between several treatment options that are in common use, but how should they make the choice? The problem is often not the absence of evidence but the absence of robust randomised controlled evidence directly comparing treatments that are already widely used in practice. Treatment options might have been directly compared with a common comparator, but not to each other; for example, in respiratory syncytial virus prevention in infants, both maternal vaccination and infant monoclonal antibodies have shown efficacy versus placebo but have not been directly compared.

articles.title: Thiol reactivity: lost in the crowd?
articles.abstract: Predictions of cysteine reactivity rely heavily on acidity (pKa) data from dilute solutions. However, the intracellular milieu is crowded and dynamic, with substrates, cofactors, and metabolites that modulate reactivity, thereby affecting cell signaling and metabolic adaptation. This forum argues that Cys pKa values are necessary but insufficient, proposing an integrated, microenvironment-dependent framework.

articles.title: From species richness to interaction architecture
articles.abstract: Biodiversity research has long focused on the number and identity of species, but recent advances suggest that ecosystem functioning depends on how species are connected. Predicting the consequences of biodiversity loss in the Anthropocene will therefore require moving beyond inventories of species toward a predictive ecology of interaction networks.

articles.title: Orbital Coupling Engineering through P-Block Metal Doping in NiFe Layered Double Hydroxides for Enhanced Anion-Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis
articles.abstract: The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) remains a major kinetic bottleneck in anodic water splitting because of sluggish adsorption and desorption kinetics of O-containing intermediates. Optimizing the adsorption strength of various O-containing intermediates in accordance with the Sabatier principle involves the precise tuning of the active-site electronic structure. Herein, we explore a p-block metal-assisted synergism regulation strategy in NiFe layered double hydroxides (LDHs) by introducing group-13 elements (Al, Ga, In) as dopants. Among various doped LDHs, In-doped NiFe-LDH shows the highest OER activity by demanding an overpotential value of 298 mV at 10 mA/cm2 along with enhanced intrinsic turnover frequency and long-term stability. X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) reveals that In3+ preferentially occupies the Fe coordination sites, while valence-band X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (VB-XPS) confirms enhanced electronic coupling in the Ni–O–In framework. Density functional theory (DFT) additionally suggests that the In 5p orbitals strongly hybridize with the O 2p and Ni 3d states, establishing a Ni3d-O2p-In5p electronic interaction that regulates the Ni electronic structure and optimizes the adsorption energies of O-containing intermediates. The resulting d-p-p orbital hybridization offers an efficient pathway for charge delocalization and strengthens the M–O covalency, thereby accelerating the OER kinetics. This study elucidates the structure–activity relationship and identifies p-block metal-induced orbital hybridization as an effective strategy for developing high-performance oxygen evolution electrocatalysts, offering an alternative to conventional transition-metal modification approaches.

articles.title: Synergy of Solid-State NMR and Dielectric Spectroscopy Reveals Synchronized Multi-Rotor Dynamics in Crystalline Supramolecular Gyroscopes
articles.abstract: Understanding the correlated dynamics of multiple molecular rotators in crystalline supramolecular assemblies is essential for designing functional molecular machines, yet deconvoluting the motions of distinct components remains inherently challenging due to the limitations of individual techniques. Here, we report a synergistic approach that combines solid-state Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (SSNMR) and dielectric spectroscopy to quantitatively resolve multirotor dynamics in a family of isostructural supramolecular gyroscopic complex architectures composed of alkyl ammonium, crown ether, and metal halide hydrate. SSNMR unambiguously reveals both the tert-butylammonium cation and the 18-crown-6 macrocycle as independent rotators─a distinction often ambiguous in such systems. Crucially, by correlating SSNMR-derived dynamics of the crown ether with dielectric relaxation of the coordinated water molecule, we uncover their synchronized rotation across a wide temperature range, mediated by charge-assisted hydrogen bonding. These findings reveal a cooperative multirotor gyroscopic model featuring synchronous rotation of an integrated coaxial crown ether–water–ammonium trio-rotator, accompanied by correlated alkyl reorientation. This synergy validates the dielectric relaxation principle in a complex, multirotor crystalline environment where unambiguous peak assignment has been a longstanding challenge. This work establishes a generalizable methodology for dissecting complex, multicomponent dynamics in crystalline materials, directly bridging molecular-scale motion to macroscopic dielectric response.

articles.title: Clarifying the Clinical Relevance of V Waves
Prominent V Waves Augment Right Ventricular Afterload Independent of the Lung Vessels in Heart Failure: Implications for Clinical Assessment of Pulmonary Vascular Disease
articles.abstract: Left atrial (LA) stiffening augments the LA V wave, pressurizing the pulmonary artery (PA) out of proportion to left ventricular end-diastolic pressure. We characterized the pathophysiologic, diagnostic, and clinical implications of LA stiffening, as defined by prominent V waves, in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. In this retrospective cohort study, patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and less than moderate mitral regurgitation at rest underwent invasive hemodynamic exercise testing. Patients with heightened operant LA stiffening were defined by the PA wedge pressure (PAWP) V wave exceeding mean PAWP by ≥10 mm Hg. A previously used formula for V wave–corrected PAWP was validated against the PAWP waveform pressure-time-area to explore impact of the V wave on transpulmonary pressure gradients. Clinical, echocardiographic, hemodynamic, and outcome data were compared for patients with and without prominent V waves. Compared with patients without prominent V waves (n=844, 79%), those with prominent V waves (n=225, 21%) were older and more likely to be women, with more severe LA myopathy, evidenced by greater LA volume index (42.2±15.0 versus 32.5±13.0 mL/m 2 , P <0.001), lower LA reservoir strain (16.4±7.5% versus 23.2±8.3%, P <0.001), more atrial fibrillation (61.3% versus 22.9%, P <0.001), and increased operant LA reservoir stiffness (0.59±0.25 versus 0.23±0.24 mm Hg/mL, P <0.001). Patients with prominent V waves had markedly higher PA systolic pressure than those without (54±16 versus 38±12 mm Hg, P <0.001) despite no difference in end-diastolic PAWP-PA pressure gradient (3±5 versus 3±4 mm Hg, P =0.950). Incorporating the V wave into PAWP improved correlation between directly measured PAWP pressure-time integral compared with mid–A wave PAWP (R 2 =0.96 versus R 2 =0.86, P <0.001 for comparison). In patients with prominent V waves, the prevalence of combined pre- and postcapillary pulmonary hypertension decreased from 60.2% to 29.3% after V wave correction for the transpulmonary pressure gradients. Despite similar corrected pulmonary vascular resistances in patients with and without prominent V waves, apparent PA compliance was much lower in patients with prominent V waves (3.03±1.56 versus 4.90±2.27 mL/mm Hg, P <0.001), augmenting right ventricular afterload, and these changes were coupled with more severe right ventricular dysfunction, tricuspid regurgitation, blunted cardiopulmonary exercise reserve, and increased risk of hospitalization for heart failure or death in patients with versus without prominent V waves (adjusted hazard ratio, 2.09 [95% CI, 1.53–2.86]; P <0.001). More than 1 in 5 patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction display prominent V waves in excess of end-diastolic PAWP. This augments right ventricular afterload due to backward transmission of the V wave, contributing to right heart failure that is independent of the pulmonary vasculature. Failure to account for the V wave during hemodynamic assessment overestimates the severity of pulmonary vascular disease present.

articles.title: Drought and soil macrofauna functional diversity effects on Mediterranean tree growth in an Ecotron ecosystem experiment
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract The intensity, frequency and severity of drought events are projected to increase in the Mediterranean region under ongoing climate change. This may impact plant growth and survival in Mediterranean forests leading to altered ecosystem dynamics. The functional diversity of soil macrofauna may have a critical role in mitigating negative climate change effects as it determines soil structure and regulates biogeochemical cycling as well as water retention. However, very little is known on how changes in climate and soil biodiversity conjointly influence plant growth. In a 5‐year experiment, we tested two levels of soil macrofauna functional diversity (Low and High), using combinations of endogeic and anecic earthworms, diplopods and isopods, and measured growth and biomass allocation in three tree species (Acer monspessulanum, Arbutus unedo and Quercus pubescens) as well as total tree biomass production. Our results showed that tree growth was overall only moderately affected by stronger drought and functional diversity of soil macrofauna. The effects of functional diversity of soil macrofauna differed among tree species. High functional diversity was associated with greater stem diameter in Q. pubescens. In contrast, low functional diversity was associated with greater stem diameter in A. unedo and proportionally greater biomass allocation to roots in A. monspessulanum. Individual macrofauna groups had stronger effects than overall functional diversity. Endogeic earthworm presence was associated with greater ecosystem‐level fine root and total plant biomass, but with lower fine root and total biomass in A. unedo. Diplopod presence was associated with greater stem diameter and higher total tree biomass in Q. pubescens. Overall, four consecutive summers of intensified drought had few significant effects on tree growth and biomass production, possibly because of high variability among individual trees. Most macrofauna effects were independent of drought, although drought modified the effect of diplopods on ecosystem‐level shoot biomass. These results show that macrofauna effects on tree growth depend on both macrofauna group and tree species identity. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.

articles.title: HGTScanner: Detecting horizontal gene transfer at the fine scale using whole organelle genomes
articles.abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has profoundly shaped eukaryotic organellar genomes like plant mitochondria. Yet no generalized tools are currently available to efficiently characterize HGT across these genomes due to both high structural complexity and low sequence divergence compared to prokaryotic HGTs. Accurate identification of HGT, including the genomic location and donor lineage, is critical for understanding its impact on genetic novelty and genome evolution as well as species interactions that generate HGTs. Here, we introduce HGTScanner, a Python tool to characterize HGT across whole organellar genomes. HGTScanner automatically establishes homology, produces alignments and phylogenies, and tests hypotheses of HGT based on BLAST, phylogeny and synteny. It contains a built‐in database of green plant (Viridiplantae) organellar sequences to facilitate the characterization of promiscuous mitochondrial HGTs and mitochondrial plastid DNAs (MTPTs) in plants but may also be adapted to other organisms like fungi which share many similar genomic features. Using benchmark data from the early diverging angiosperm Amborella and parasitic plant Orobanchaceae, we demonstrate that HGTScanner can effectively locate and identify the donor lineages of MTPT and HGT. In Amborella, we recovered the well‐documented fusion of moss and green algae mitochondria, and discovered prevalent HGTs from the New Caledonian parasitic plant Hachettea (Mystropetalaceae). In the parasitic Orobanchaceae, non‐native MTPTs are strongly linked with their sympatrically distributed host plants. HGTScanner is an efficient and flexible tool that can drive discoveries of HGT without a priori knowledge regarding the donor identity. The sympatric distribution of donor‐recipient pairs in HGT events suggests that HGTs can serve as valuable genetic markers for organismal interactions across time and terrain.

articles.title: Limited Lifetime Costs of Inbreeding in a Large Wild Population of Superb Fairy‐Wrens
articles.abstract: Inbreeding depression can have major negative effects on both individual fitness and population performance. The impact of inbreeding depression in wild populations remains poorly understood, and our knowledge is primarily based on estimations in insular populations with limited dispersal, which has been predicted to enhance the capacity for outcrossing. Limited migration and small population sizes, which make insular and endangered populations tractable models for fieldwork, often experience low genetic variation and may be subject to stronger inbreeding effects. Estimating inbreeding effects is difficult in many populations because pedigrees of migrants are unknown. Genomic data offer methods to estimate realised inbreeding even in migrants. Here, we apply genomic methods to a superb fairy‐wren (Malurus cyaneus) population that has been subject to detailed study of fitness variation over three decades. The population has sex‐biased dispersal, resulting in many immigrant females. We use genomic inbreeding estimates to explicitly test for inbreeding depression across several key components of individual fitness, including nestling condition, juvenile survival and adult traits. Genomic methods were able to recover previous pedigree‐based findings of inbreeding depression in early nestling condition and additionally identified some evidence for inbreeding depression in fledgling but not juvenile mortality. The only adult fitness trait affected, male extra‐pair paternity, is highly variable and under strong sexual selection. Our findings suggest that natural populations experiencing high effective population sizes and regular dispersal might be less affected by inbreeding depression than previously assumed based on studies of often insular and smaller populations.

articles.title: High-output elastomeric SBS/PAN piezoelectric nanofibrous membranes via thermal engineering
[Editorial] Rethinking threats to human survival
articles.abstract: Much health advocacy is driven by single-issue activism. Communities with a common interest—from AIDS to child health, climate to tobacco control—focus intensely on their own domain. And understandably so. Important progress has been made through often courageous direct action. But this sharply competitive approach is, according to a new Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health, dangerously flawed. Indeed, perhaps the most important contribution of this Commission is to move global health beyond the consideration of individual harms.

articles.title: [Health Policy] Strengthening health systems to prioritise, provide care, and prevent osteoarthritis: a roadmap for global health policy
articles.abstract: By 2050, almost 1 billion people are expected to live with osteoarthritis—a disabling musculoskeletal condition with currently no cure. Despite its burden and costs, osteoarthritis remains largely invisible in national and global health agendas, is poorly integrated within service models for other chronic health conditions, and is frequently perceived as inevitable with ageing and associated with limited therapeutic options. This context drives an osteoarthritis identity problem that fuels frustration among those living with the disease and health-care professionals, perpetuates stigma and inequities, undermines access to effective interventions, and crucially, deprioritises osteoarthritis in health policy.

articles.title: Emerging trends in redox-neutral phosphorus(V) organocatalysis
articles.abstract: Phosphorus-mediated reactions that leverage the thermodynamic driving force of phosphorus(III) oxidation are crucial in all areas of the chemical industry. While substantial progress has been made in phosphorus(III/V) redox organocatalysis to develop catalytic alternatives, the rising field of redox-neutral phosphorus(V) organocatalysis has revealed new modes of phosphorus-based reactivity in chemical transformations without requiring stoichiometric reductants. This review highlights key advances in redox-neutral phosphorus(V) organocatalysis with a focus on fundamental phosphorus(V) reactivity, organized by the catalyst structure and emphasizing its role as a Lewis acid, Brønsted acid/base, nucleophile, superbase, or single-electron transfer agent. We close with remarks connecting established reactivity paradigms that will likely be applied to new generations of phosphorus(V) catalysts capable of solving modern synthetic challenges.

articles.title: Formamidinium-Solvent Intermediates Mediate Self-Seeding Crystallization for Efficient Inverted α-FAPbI3 Perovskite Solar Cells
articles.abstract: Formamidinium lead iodide (FAPbI3) perovskites are promising for high-performance solar cells; however, the low surface energy of self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) impedes α-phase nucleation in inverted devices. Here, we report a formamidinium (FA)-solvent intermediate-mediated self-seeding crystallization strategy to enable quality α-phase FAPbI3. By employing N-formylmorpholine (NFM) as a non-toxic solvent, (FA···NFM)PbI3 intermediates are formed, thereby lowering the phase-transition barrier and promoting the spontaneous formation of α-phase nuclei at the early stage of crystallization. These preformed nuclei serve as intrinsic seeds, facilitating rapid nucleation and orientated crystal growth. Consequently, NFM-based devices achieve efficiencies of 26.41% and 26.56% using 2-methoxyethanol (2-Me) and N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) as primary solvents, respectively, with a 1 cm2 device reaching 25.47%. The unencapsulated devices retain 85% and 90% of their initial efficiencies after 1200 h illumination and 1400 h thermal aging at 85 °C, respectively.

articles.title: Improving the Calendar Life of Silicon Anodes with Inorganic Solid–Electrolyte Interphases
articles.abstract: Silicon anodes unlock higher energy density in Li-ion batteries but suffer from poor calendar life due to inadequately passivating solid–electrolyte interphases (SEIs). Here, we contrast the calendar aging behaviors of single- and mixed-salt locally superconcentrated electrolytes (LSCEs) against carbonate electrolytes. Mixed-salt LSCE cells retained 96% and 44% of precalendar capacity after one month and then after five months, while carbonate electrolyte cells retained 77% and 1%, respectively. The mixed-salt LSCE advantage is tied to the formation of a predominantly inorganic SEI, evidenced by nanoscale Fourier transform infrared spectromicroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and 3D time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry. After 5 months, however, perturbations to SEIs were evident in all cells, accelerating voltage decay and capacity loss by lithium inventory loss associated with SEI growth. These findings suggest that future electrolytes may benefit from strategies that continuously reinforce the SEI through controlled anion and solvent redox in LSCEs.

Practical Considerations for Operando 7Li Nuclear Magnetic Resonance in Coin and Pouch Cells
articles.abstract: Operando nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy provides unique insight into chemical changes in batteries during use but has largely been limited to custom plastic cells. Unfortunately, the metal casings that house commercial batteries distort and shield radiofrequency (RF) fields required for excitation and detection in NMR. Here, we use operando7Li NMR spectroscopy to study metal-encased batteries in both coin and pouch cell formats without modifying the cell or casing. We benchmark NMR spectra obtained from stainless-steel coin cells and aluminum-laminate pouch cells to plastic coin cells and show that casing composition, auxiliary hardware, and sample placement strongly influence observed shift, signal intensity, and line shape due to bulk magnetic susceptibility effects and RF attenuation upon interacting with cell parts. These effects are most severe in stainless-steel coin cells (and in particular 304-grade stainless steel) but can be mitigated through the use of Al spacers while retaining the stainless-steel caps and springs. In light of these considerations, we leverage operando7Li NMR to track lithium plating/stripping and monitor the accumulation of electrochemically inactive “dead” lithium (Li0) during galvanostatic cycling in coin and pouch cells. In pouch cells, the lean electrolyte volume allows us to resolve changes in the 7Li electrolyte signal during formation that are consistent with electrolyte redistribution and wetting. Taken together, these results demonstrate how to alter cell susceptibility to improve NMR signals during operando measurements in commercially relevant form factors while also establishing the cell design constraints that limit quantitative interpretation.

articles.title: Unraveling the Mystery of Near-Infrared Emission in an Antimony Halide Dimer Driven by the Jahn–Teller Effect
articles.abstract: Most zero-dimensional hybrid metal halides enable emission in the first near-infrared (NIR-I) region (650–950 nm), and the shorter wavelengths result in poor photon penetration depth. Here, we report the observation of an NIR-II emission signal (band gap = 1.13 eV) from a (BTBAC)2Sb2Cl8 single crystal at room temperature. Although a variety of mechanisms are involved in the explanation of such a broad band with a large Stokes shift, the exploration of the structural origin of the NIR optical activity remains challenging due to misconceptions about excitons and experimental limitations. A strategy that spatially confines 5s2 ions within edge-shared [Sb2Cl8]2– units with controlled lattice distortion is proposed to cause a Jahn–Teller effect (JTE) during the interconfiguration transition (3P1 → 1S0). A family of hybrid metal halides doped with Bi3+,In3+ or Bi3+/In3+ demonstrates that the fine interplay between the Jahn–Teller effect and spin–orbit coupling (SOC) takes into full consideration orbital degeneracy and electron flipping, thus boosting the photoluminescence quantum yield to 12%. TD-DFT calculations visualize the symmetry of the two lattices within a dimeric structure varying with specific modes, and the rational assignment of the energy gap (ground state: 3.69 eV; excited state: 1.22 eV) between 1S0 and 3P1 is highly consistent with the experimental findings (λex = 330 nm; λem = 1100 nm). Leveraging the (BTBAC)2Sb2Cl8 sample, electroluminescence pumped by a UV-LED chip yields a highly efficient NIR-II emission, and the phosphor displays diverse functions in night vision and anticounterfeiting.

Shrubs benefit from being functionally more conservative and distinct from neighbour trees
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Multi‐strata forests can enhance ecosystem functioning, with interactions between overstorey trees and understorey shrubs playing a pivotal role. However, how the structure and composition of neighbouring trees, together with shrub traits, influence shrub growth remains poorly understood. In a large‐scale subtropical biodiversity experiment manipulating tree and shrub species richness, we inventoried 4411 shrubs and their surrounding trees after 11 years of interactions. We found that individual shrub biomass declined with increasing neighbour tree species richness, basal area and functional diversity, but exhibited a U‐shaped trend with the proportion of ectomycorrhizal‐associated neighbour tree individuals. Shrubs with more conservative resource‐use strategies attained higher biomass, particularly when surrounded by trees with low functional diversity and a high proportion of ectomycorrhizal associations. Biomass was also greater when shrubs were more resource‐conservative and functionally distinct from the neighbouring trees. Our findings highlight how shrub functional traits, combined with tree diversity, competition and functional traits, shape tree–shrub interactions, with shrubs benefiting more from resource‐conservative and functionally distinct traits relative to their neighbouring trees. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.

articles.title: Why don't all birds lay early? Causes and consequences of breeding timing for a long‐lived migratory seabird
articles.abstract: Why don't all birds lay early? Our 16‐year study of Manx shearwater behaviour shows that selection on breeding timing fluctuates among years. We also find that lay dates are influenced by persistent individual differences, variation in non‐breeding duration, and pair synchrony, potentially constraining breeding phenological advancement under ongoing climate change. Abstract The relationship between earlier laying and higher breeding success is well‐established in avian species. However, a wide distribution of breeding timings is often maintained within a population, and the causes and consequences of this variation require further exploration, particularly as many avian species advance breeding phenology in response to climate change. Using a 16‐year dataset combining colony observations and biologging of Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus), we show that earlier laying does not always result in higher breeding success, with later laying becoming less costly in recent years. We additionally report a slight advancement in breeding timing within breeding pairs, despite finding no temporal trends in spring bloom onset. Nonetheless, birds adjusted lay date in response to interannual variation in phytoplankton bloom timing, and years with stronger Celtic Sea blooms exhibited stronger selection for early breeding. Breeding timing was also influenced by repeatable individual differences in migratory behaviour, with birds undertaking generally earlier, shorter migrations to less southerly destinations laying earlier across years. However, lay date was not determined solely by individual behaviour. In this long‐lived species with stable pair bonds, the arrival date of the second‐returning bird constrained advancement in laying. This study suggests that variation in breeding timing is maintained through the combined effects of fluctuating selection, persistent individual differences, variation in non‐breeding duration and pair‐level processes. articles.abstract: The Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health's report by Christopher J L Murray and colleagues uses forecasts based on expected cumulative amenable disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) to quantify and compare threats from 2025 to 2100.1 The Commission's intent is to equip governments with the tools to make smart long-term decisions that reduce risk based on “systematic, repeatable risk assessment and preparedness planning” as opposed to “short-termism and localism”.

articles.title: [Perspectives] John Wong: making an impact on population health at scale
articles.abstract: “I’m concerned that the narrative now around ageing populations is one of doom and gloom. But long-lived populations are not the problem. The problem is that we haven’t allowed people to get to an older age healthy”, says John Wong, Executive Director of the Centre for Population Health at the National University of Singapore (NUS) and Executive Director of The Yong Pung How and Yong Wei-Woo Centre at the National University Health System (NUHS), Singapore. “Two-thirds of the world is now below the fertility replacement rate, and unless we keep our populations healthy throughout their whole lifespan, we’ll have this major challenge of more and more unwell older people”, continued Wong, who is also Isabel Chan Professor in Medical Sciences in the Division of Haematology-Oncology at the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, NUS, and Emeritus Consultant in the Department of Haematology-Oncology, National University Cancer Institute, NUHS, Singapore.

articles.title: [Review] Addressing threats to future global health—what is the right timeframe?
articles.abstract: Our decisions today can support or threaten future human health. Insofar as we protect the planet or invest in fruitful research on pandemic countermeasures, we promote future wellbeing and health, sometimes at the present generation's expense. As we warm the planet, accelerate antibiotic resistance, or consume finite natural resources, we might serve present-day wellbeing or health at the expense of future generations. To decide which such trade-offs are legitimate or advisable, we need to know how to balance the health interests of future generations against each other and against our own.

articles.title: [The Lancet Commissions] The Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health
articles.abstract: This report from the Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health lays out a foresight-driven, health-focused approach to identifying and prioritising major threats to global health over the remainder of the century. We argue that recent global shocks (including COVID-19, Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease, major geopolitical conflict, accelerating climate impacts, rapid shifts in development assistance, and the emergence of powerful artificial intelligence [AI] systems) show how quickly assumptions about stability can be overturned—and why governments and multilateral institutions must counter short-termism and localism with systematic, repeatable risk assessment and preparedness planning.

articles.title: Pioneering MOF-303 in Lithium–Sulfur Batteries: Coordination Defect Engineering Enables Accelerated Sulfur Redox and Dendrite-Free Plating
articles.abstract: Lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries are severely hindered by the shuttle effect of lithium polysulfides (LiPSs) and uncontrolled lithium dendrite growth. Herein, a defect-engineered MOF-303 (D-MOF-303) modified separator is developed via a ball-milling strategy to simultaneously mitigate both issues, marking the first application of MOF-303 in the Li–S battery field. The intentional introduction of ligand defects and oxygen vacancies reduces particle size, establishes a hierarchical porous structure, and amplifies local Lewis acidity. Consequently, the D-MOF-303 coating layer provides exceptional chemisorption and accelerated electrocatalytic conversion kinetics for LiPSs, while concurrently homogenizing lithium-ion flux to achieve long-term dendrite-free lithium plating. Benefiting from these synergistic merits, the resulting Li–S full cells exhibit high capacity retention over 500 cycles at 0.5 C, enhanced rate capability up to 3 C, and notable environmental resilience under high-humidity aging conditions. This work demonstrates the potential of coordination defect engineering in metal–organic frameworks for advancing high-energy-density and commercially viable energy storage technologies.
